_Why does a better model not, by itself, make a better machine?_

The learned model is the part of a physical machine that is easiest to improve and easiest to score, so it attracts most of the effort. Useful service depends on everything around it as well. The body must sustain the task across loads, surfaces, and hours of duty, the learned behavior must hold in the states its own actions create, each proposal must be admitted, corrected, or refused before the motion it asks for is already under way, and the evidence for all of it must match the conditions of operation and stay true as the machine and its site change. Each of these can be engineered well in isolation while the machine as a whole remains unjustified, because doubt accumulates across every premise a physical claim depends on, and a premise that no one names or owns is assumed silently. A team that cannot join these parts into one argument keeps improving the model while an unmeasured floor, an unqualified detector, or an unowned restriction decides what the machine actually does. The same joined argument also chooses what to build next, since the most valuable measurement, experience, or design change is the one that retires the weakest open premise. At the causal boundary, irreversibility makes that weakest premise, not the best prediction, the measure of what a machine may be trusted to do.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain why a better prediction can still produce a worse physical action, and synthesize the four laws into the design argument that answers it
- Place current learned proposers in the move from prediction to action, and explain why more capable proposers do not move the permission decision into the model
- Apply the four laws to select and evaluate a candidate operating mode for an unfamiliar machine
- Distinguish proposer autonomy, whole-machine task success, and protection when assessing a completed design
- Construct residual-claims entries with supported restrictions, accountable owners, and predeclared closure tests
- Select the next measurement, learning experiment, or design change needed to extend a machine's capability
:::
## From a Better Prediction to Useful Service {#sec-frontier-architectural-synthesis}

Every engineering division of this book establishes a distinct operational claim about a system whose learned outputs drive physical actions: what its mechanical body can sustain, what its learned proposer demonstrates under closed-loop evaluation, what its execution runtime admits within strict latency deadlines, and what its accumulated evidence licenses in deployment. While individual chapters developed these subsystems in isolation, building a dependable machine requires uniting them into a coherent whole. A robust architectural synthesis must satisfy three demanding criteria. First, it must integrate these disparate claims into an end-to-end operational argument on the warehouse machine they were built around. Second, its underlying methodology must transfer cleanly to unfamiliar hardware, such as the packaging cell analyzed in @sec-frontier-generalizing-unfamiliar-systems. Third, because mechanical actions alter the physical world irreversibly, the architecture must explicitly audit its own epistemic boundaries—documenting unmeasured environmental assumptions (@sec-frontier-epistemic-limits) and providing a structured framework for evolving those assumptions into new capabilities (@sec-frontier-assumptions-change).

In @sec-boundary, we examined the central question of physical artificial intelligence: why a better prediction can still produce a worse physical action, and what the rest of the machine must supply so that speculative model proposals become useful work within justified limits. That journey began in @sec-boundary-beyond-glass by contrasting physical AI with what preceded it. Traditional machine learning evaluated advisory predictions against static datasets, and agentic machine learning deployed iterative reasoning loops within the protective sandboxes of digital software—operating behind glass with elastic virtual time, transactional rollbacks, and symbolic interfaces. Physical AI stepped through that glass into the continuous physical world, where computation commands physical actuators across the causal boundary. That transition stripped away every digital privilege, forcing computer systems engineering to confront four physical realities: inexorable continuous time where computational delay is physical distance, mechanical and thermodynamic irreversibility that forbids undo operations, single-batch real-time constraints ($B=1$), and the imperative separation between speculative proposals and deterministic permission.

That investigation centered on a single reference platform: a warehouse mobile manipulator tasked with retrieving an object from an active conveyor, opening a spring-latched cage door, and transporting the payload through an aisle shared with people. Fulfilling that mission exercises the foundational capabilities introduced in @sec-boundary: designing physical and computational dynamics, teaching learned policies, integrating real-time runtimes, evaluating closed-loop behavior, and maintaining operational safety envelopes under real-world degradation. Every design choice along this pipeline directly constrained the next.

We can now state precisely why a better prediction can produce a worse physical action: physical success depends on dynamic variables that never enter the learned model's training loss or input space. The physical distance a mobile base traverses while a neural network computes its forward pass, the friction available at the tire-floor interface during sudden braking, the cascading states into which the robot's own prior actions thrust it, and the operational shifts between demonstration datasets and live deployment conditions all dictate what an actuator command does once it crosses the causal boundary. Increasing the statistical accuracy of a model refines the proposed trajectory, but it alters none of these underlying physical, temporal, or environmental constraints.

The second half of the question—what the surrounding machine must supply—resolves into the four-step argument of @sec-boundary-central-question, aligning one engineering discipline with each governing law. Under the first law (*irreversibility*), the body's mechanical and thermal limits bound what any proposal may request. Part I translated payload capacity, surface traction, contact forces, motor heating, and energy reserves into strict operational budgets that govern proposal horizons, execution cadence, and deterministic fallback paths. Under the second law (*endogenous data*), policy competence holds only over the empirical distribution of states induced by closed-loop interaction. Part II tied proposer evaluation directly to the states the physical machine actually visits, transforming recovery failures into targeted collection regimes rather than unhandled anomalies. Under the third law (*proposal is not permission*), execution authority resides in an independent permission path rather than the learned model. Part III unified observation freshness contracts, grounded geometric targets, timed trajectories, and real-time admission filters onto a compute topology engineered to meet hard deadlines under heavy load. Under the fourth law (*evidence bounds authority*), deployment scope is bounded by qualified system-wide evidence. Part IV structured physical operation as a governed service contract that decouples proposer autonomy, whole-system task success, and protective intervention. A least-change speed filter, for example, can preserve an in-flight delivery even when a raw proposal requires intervention, whereas an emergency stop protects physical hardware without fulfilling the promised service.

When deployed on physical hardware, this framework culminates in a formal release decision rather than an informal assertion of operational capability. In the baseline audit presented in @sec-release-case-worked-full, the unmitigated system records yield a verdict of `REFUSE`, reflecting unhedged tail risks and unverified fault margins. In contrast, the stipulated branch in @sec-release-stipulated-service demonstrates how comprehensive empirical evidence elevates that status to conditional authorization (`COND`). Under those verified performance and fault distributions, the machine is licensed to execute inspected-route transport, guarded door approaches, and close-proximity handovers—provided that standing environmental conditions governing floor traction, pedestrian crossings, feeder alignment, and sensor calibration remain actively verified. This is a disciplined systems result established under stated premises rather than an ungrounded deployment claim, demonstrating the complete chain of traceability connecting high-level mission goals to concrete operating envelopes and empirical guarantees.

@Fig-17-causal-loop-synthesis diagrams this closed causal loop across five stacked architectural tiers enclosed within a standing governance envelope: at the top, the Brain proposes action chunks across the proposal boundary at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.intent_rate_str`; inside the Nervous System, an application processor forwards candidate setpoints across a black-channel link to a discrete safety microcontroller, whose permission path ticks at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.permission_str` to evaluate kinematic and dynamic invariants; admitted commands pass to the Body, where motor drives close current loops at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.current_loop_str` on a `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.bus_str` bus to exert forces and torques at the Boundary; and the evolving World returns event-timestamped measurements through sensor channels to both the fast permission filter and the Brain. Release governance establishes the static parameters, safety budgets, and standing operating envelopes across all five levels, providing an institutional framework that enforces operational boundaries without interfering with cycle-by-cycle real-time arbitration.

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-loop-figure
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CLOSED-LOOP SYNTHESIS FIGURE LABELS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-17-causal-loop-synthesis (SVG labels are hand-typed).
# │ Goal:    Keep the machine's rates and bus voltage drawn in the figure
# │          equal to the registry values the rest of the book prints.
# │ Show:    Nothing; the cell only guards the drawn labels.
# │ How:     Compare each drawn label with the registered machine value.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class LoopSynthesisFigure:
    """Values drawn in fig17_closed_loop_synthesis.svg."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Drawn labels and the registry values they must match) ──────
    drawn = {
        "intent rate (Hz)": (2.0, RM.intent_rate.to(ureg.Hz).magnitude),
        "intent inference (ms)": (336.0, RM.intent_reference_latency.to(ureg.ms).magnitude),
        "chunk renewal (ms)": (50.0, (1 / RM.chunk_rate).to(ureg.ms).magnitude),
        "setpoint step (ms)": (25.0, RM.chunk_step.to(ureg.ms).magnitude),
        "permission tick (kHz)": (1.0, RM.permission_rate.to(ureg.kHz).magnitude),
        "drive bus nominal (V)": (47.7, RM.drive_bus_nominal.to(ureg.volt).magnitude),
        "drive current loop (kHz)": (20.0, RM.current_loop_rate.to(ureg.kHz).magnitude),
    }

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    for _name, (_label, _value) in drawn.items():
        check(abs(_label - _value) < 1e-9, f"closed-loop figure label for {_name} is stale ({_label} vs {_value})")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    intent_rate_str = fmt_frequency(RM.intent_rate, unit=ureg.Hz, precision=0)
    renewal_str = fmt_latency(1 / RM.chunk_rate, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    setpoint_str = fmt_latency(RM.chunk_step, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    permission_str = fmt_frequency(RM.permission_rate, unit=ureg.kHz, precision=0)
    bus_str = fmt_voltage(RM.drive_bus_nominal, precision=1)
    current_loop_str = fmt_frequency(RM.current_loop_rate, unit=ureg.kHz, precision=0)
```

::: {#fig-17-causal-loop-synthesis fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Closed causal loop**: The Brain proposes across the proposal boundary, and the permission path in the Nervous System admits, modifies, or refuses each proposal before the Body acts. The Body's current becomes force and motion at the Boundary, the World evolves, and the Boundary returns measurements with capture times to the permission path and the Brain. Not every state of the World reaches a sensor. The governance envelope surrounds all five levels and changes on the timescale of releases rather than control cycles. The labels are this machine's values: the intent model proposes at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.intent_rate_str`, the chunk is renewed every `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.renewal_str`, the application processor sends a setpoint every `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.setpoint_str` over a black-channel link to a discrete safety MCU whose permission path ticks at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.permission_str`, and the drives close their current loops at `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.current_loop_str` from a `{python} LoopSynthesisFigure.bus_str` bus. Arrows run from the Brain to the application processor, labeled proposal, from the safety MCU to the Body, labeled admitted command, and on to the World, labeled current in a winding and force and motion. A return arrow runs from the World to the Boundary, then up a side lane to the safety MCU, labeled fresh state, and to the Brain, labeled observations. Labels give the intent model 2 Hz with 336 ms inference, chunk renewal every 50 ms, a setpoint every 25 ms, a 1 kHz permission tick, a 20 kHz current loop in the drives, and a 47.7 V drive bus; the Boundary is event-timed, the World is continuous, and governance has no control rate."}

The records summarized in @tbl-17-master-synthesis bring these four governing laws into an integrated engineering workflow. Rather than treating safety as an abstract property of a model, each architectural division produces durable, auditable artifacts that preserve empirical evidence and operational intent when tasks, payloads, or environmental conditions change.

\Needspace{25\baselineskip}

| Law                            | Part                                                                                             | Records that carry it                                                                                        | Condition to maintain                                                                                                                                 | Engineering result                                                                                                             |
|:-------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Irreversibility**            | I (@sec-body, @sec-brain, @sec-nervous)                                                          | Limit records (@sec-body); the proposer's limits (@sec-brain), which enter the handoff record (@sec-nervous) | Each measured limit, such as floor friction, payload, brake onset, or observation age, still holds under present conditions                           | A feasible speed or force envelope, a timed proposal interface, and a reachable fallback                                       |
| **Endogenous data**            | II (@sec-data, @sec-training, @sec-evaluation)                                                   | Demonstration provenance record, policy manifest, evaluation record                                          | The states the machine enters lie inside the target operational design domain (ODD, @sec-data-policy-coverage) that closed-loop evaluation represents | A learned behavior evaluated in its closed loop; new qualified experience can expand its supported task population             |
| **Proposal is not permission** | III (@sec-perception, @sec-memory, @sec-intent, @sec-planning, @sec-enforcement, @sec-placement) | Observation contract, belief record, intent lease, trajectory record, enforcement record, placement record   | The permission path sees fresh, distinguishable state and meets its deadline under load                                                               | Useful motion admitted or minimally corrected within current limits; invalid active authority invokes a state-matched fallback |
| **Evidence bounds authority**  | IV (@sec-intervention, @sec-verification, @sec-release)                                          | Authority record, fault record, release manifest, and the residual-claims register of this chapter           | The premises of the release claim still hold after release                                                                                            | A named service authorized under standing conditions, with tested intervention and update procedures                           |

: **The four laws as engineering competence**: Each part produces records that support the next design decision. The conditions and results belong to the particular machine and its evidence; they are not universal hardware requirements. {#tbl-17-master-synthesis tbl-colwidths="[14,17,25,22,22]"}

This architectural synthesis also illuminates the historical trajectory traced in @sec-boundary-prediction-to-action. Over eight decades, machine learning has steadily migrated from the periphery toward raw actuation: evolving from purely deterministic mechanisms, to learned perceptual frontends feeding analytical planners, to end-to-end motor policies, and ultimately to foundation models that propose action chunks across heterogeneous robotic embodiments. With each transition, safety guarantees that once relied on physical isolation or vigilant human operators had to be internalized within the computational stack itself.

The warehouse platform exemplifies this modern equilibrium. Its hierarchical split between an intent model proposing at 2 Hz and an action-chunk policy operating at higher frequencies mirrors contemporary vision-language-action pipelines, yet the safety guarantees displaced by these statistical models are preserved by the deterministic architecture surrounding them. The reflex halts beneath Shakey's STRIPS planner and the persistent low-level behaviors of Brooks's subsumption architecture have evolved into our discrete permission path, governed by mathematically signed kinematic and dynamic envelopes tailored to this mechanical body. Similarly, the safety pilot who hovered near the loop during the DARPA Robotics Challenge has been transformed into a formal intervention authority equipped with deterministic handover budgets, while the environmental oversight once provided by a human operator is now codified as explicit standing release conditions.

The next evolutionary phase, highlighted by the open challenges in @sec-frontier-four-open-challenges, involves foundation models that control diverse physical bodies while continuously learning from fleet-wide deployments. While cross-embodiment pretraining broadens model capabilities, it also stretches the model further beyond the empirical distribution of any single operating environment. Expanding what a proposer can suggest makes an independent permission path even more critical. Granting a learned model greater proposing latitude demands more rigorous dynamic verification at runtime and more defensible empirical evidence at release—a principle directly reflected in the European machinery regulations examined in @sec-frontier-thesis-in-law.

This systems architecture provides an engineering method designed to generalize across platforms. The transferable core consists of the foundational questions, dynamic budgets, empirical protocols, and interface boundaries; the platform-specific elements are the calibrated numerical thresholds, kinematic envelopes, and actuator limits. Applying this framework to the packaging cell in @sec-frontier-generalizing-unfamiliar-systems demonstrates how these invariant principles adapt when mechanics, cycle frequencies, and operational environments change.
## Generalizing to Unfamiliar Systems {#sec-frontier-generalizing-unfamiliar-systems}

When an automated packaging cell shuttles containers, closes closure tabs, and repeats high-rate cycles across a full shift, it operates against strict physical limits: kinematic reach, contact force, and thermal buildup in the drive motors. Building such an embodied system requires pairing a capable learned proposer with an execution pipeline whose runtime authority respects those physical bounds. The four bedrock laws of @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws formalize this engineering discipline. Together, they trace an unbroken chain from the task's irreversible consequences to measurable physical envelopes, through the closed-loop data required to train and validate policies, down to the real-time runtime that gates motor commands, and ultimately to the operational envelope certified for deployment. Applying this four-law framework to a novel packaging cell demonstrates how the systems principles developed throughout this book generalize far beyond the warehouse mobile manipulator.

### The four-law audit protocol for novel physical systems {#sec-frontier-four-law-audit-protocol}

The audit proceeds through a disciplined sequence. It begins by identifying the irreversible physical consequences of the intended task—the kinematic collisions, plastic structural deformations, and thermal overloads that no control command can undo—and establishing the measurable bounds that define a safe operational envelope. These physical boundaries directly dictate the data-collection campaign: training demonstrations and closed-loop evaluations must reflect the actual dynamics that safety limiters will permit. Next, the learned policy integrates with an independent permission path whose timing budgets, sensor observations, and deterministic fallbacks match the physical plant. Finally, end-to-end qualification of the integrated machine establishes the operational boundaries under which the system may safely execute. Because each layer constrains the next, adjustments ripple upstream; reducing the permitted transit speed to satisfy a stopping budget, for example, alters the visual flow and dynamic distribution that the learning pipeline must master.

### Multi-archetype case study on automated packaging cells {#sec-frontier-packaging-cell-study}

Consider an automated parcel induction and sortation cell operating inside a high-throughput logistics hub. The machine shuttles shipping containers along a linear track, actuates an articulated insertion head onto container flaps to engage structural retention tabs, and drives high-rate linear servo drives through rapid, cyclic acceleration profiles. This single workcell couples all three physical machine classes of @sec-boundary-three-classes within a single enclosure: the carriage as moving mass, the insertion head as contact force, and the high-duty actuator drives as thermal dissipation.

The first law focuses on what the machine cannot undo. We therefore begin by cataloging the cell's irreversible state changes\index{State change!irreversible} alongside the governing physical bounds\index{Physical bounds}. A loaded parcel container traversing a linear transfer rail carries momentum. When a carriage strikes an obstruction, kinetic energy dissipates through plastic deformation of the container and structural deflection of the frame—a mechanical state transition that cannot be reversed by commanding the drive motor in reverse. The insertion mechanism introduces a second irreversible boundary: an actuator drives a mechanical tool head against package tabs to lock retaining clips. If the actuator exerts force beyond the compressive load capacity of the carton wall, the container buckles, crushing internal contents. The high-duty drive introduces a third irreversible boundary through Joule heating ($I^2 R$). Continuous high-acceleration cycles pump thermal energy into sealed motor windings. Winding insulation does not need to melt to fail; elevated temperatures accelerate chemical degradation over time, shortening insulation life rapidly [@iec60085-2007]. Cooling the housing afterward cannot restore the dielectric strength already lost. Because the damage accumulates monotonically across duty cycles, an instantaneous temperature trip threshold alone cannot bound it.

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-packaging-stop
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PACKAGING CELL: A CANDIDATE TRANSPORT MODE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-frontier-packaging-cell-study.
# │ Goal:    Test nominal speed against a fixed stop line, solve the speed
# │          ceiling the stop budget admits, and check a restricted speed below it.
# │ Show:    Delay, stopping distances, the ceiling, reserve, and translational energy.
# │ How:     One-off hypothetical scenario inputs; MLSysIM constant-deceleration
# │          stopping (calc_safe_stopping_distance), its positive root
# │          (calc_max_permitted_velocity), and kinetic-energy models. These are
# │          not measurements.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class PackagingCell:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario assumptions) ───────────────────────────────────────
    mass = 12 * ureg.kg  # scenario assumption: total moving mass, including load
    v_nom = 1.5 * ureg.meter / ureg.second  # scenario assumption: nominal speed
    v_clamp = 0.5 * ureg.meter / ureg.second  # scenario assumption: restricted speed
    clearance = 60 * ureg.mm  # scenario assumption: clearance to a fixed stop line
    reserve = 15 * ureg.mm  # scenario assumption: allocated uncertainty and clearance reserve
    deceleration = 15 * ureg.meter / ureg.second**2  # scenario assumption: braking lower bound after delay
    exposure = 16 * ureg.ms  # scenario assumption: worst-case event-to-usable-frame interval
    processing = 36 * ureg.ms  # scenario assumption: transfer, inference, scheduling, and admission
    bus = 2 * ureg.ms  # scenario assumption: admitted command to brake-driver delivery
    onset = 10 * ureg.ms  # scenario assumption: delivery to full assumed deceleration
    check_rate = 1 * ureg.kHz  # scenario assumption: independent kinematic-check rate
    force_cap = 220 * ureg.N  # scenario assumption: selected limiter setting, not material strength
    temperature_trip = Q_(105, ureg.degC)  # scenario assumption: selected sensor threshold
    stall_timeout = 400 * ureg.ms  # scenario assumption: selected stall-detection timeout
    bus_trip = 60 * ureg.volt  # scenario assumption: selected inverter overvoltage threshold
    deceleration_check = 12 * ureg.meter / ureg.second**2  # scenario assumption: a lower qualified braking bound (checkpoint estimate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    delay = exposure + processing + bus + onset
    stop_budget = clearance - reserve
    blind_nom = v_nom * delay
    brake_nom = v_nom**2 / (2 * deceleration)
    stop_nom = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_nom, delay, deceleration)
    deficit = stop_nom - clearance
    # Speed ceiling: positive root of v tau + v^2/(2a) = clearance - reserve
    v_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(clearance, delay, deceleration, physical_margin=reserve).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second)
    # What changes if: halve the processing allocation, or halve the braking bound
    v_ceiling_fast_proc = calc_max_permitted_velocity(clearance, exposure + processing / 2 + bus + onset, deceleration, physical_margin=reserve).to(
        ureg.meter / ureg.second
    )
    v_ceiling_half_decel = calc_max_permitted_velocity(clearance, delay, deceleration / 2, physical_margin=reserve).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second)
    blind_clamp = v_clamp * delay
    brake_clamp = v_clamp**2 / (2 * deceleration)
    stop_clamp = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_clamp, delay, deceleration)
    remaining = clearance - stop_clamp
    energy_nom = calc_kinetic_energy(mass, v_nom)
    energy_clamp = calc_kinetic_energy(mass, v_clamp)
    energy_reduction = (1 - energy_clamp / energy_nom).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    # Operands of the positive root, shown in the notebook
    a_tau = (deceleration * delay).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second)
    two_a_d = (2 * deceleration * stop_budget).to(ureg.meter**2 / ureg.second**2)
    root_term = ((a_tau**2 + two_a_d) ** 0.5).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second)
    v_ceiling_check = calc_max_permitted_velocity(clearance, delay, deceleration_check, physical_margin=reserve).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # 2026-09-28: pin the complete hypothetical budget and the claimed reserve.
    check(delay == 64 * ureg.ms, "All four delay allocations must total 64 ms.")
    check(blind_nom > clearance, "Nominal speed must exhaust clearance before braking.")
    check(abs(stop_nom.to(ureg.mm).magnitude - 171) < 1e-9, "Nominal stop must be 171 mm.")
    check(abs(stop_clamp.to(ureg.mm).magnitude - 40.3333333333) < 1e-6, "Restricted stop must be 40.3 mm.")
    check(stop_clamp < stop_budget and remaining > reserve, "Restricted stop must preserve the allocated reserve.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling.magnitude - 0.5471) < 5e-4, "Carriage speed ceiling must be 0.55 m/s.")
    check(
        abs(calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_ceiling, delay, deceleration).to(ureg.mm).magnitude - stop_budget.to(ureg.mm).magnitude) < 1e-6,
        "At the ceiling the stop must fill the stop budget exactly.",
    )
    check(v_clamp < v_ceiling < v_nom, "The restricted speed is chosen below the ceiling, which sits below nominal.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling_fast_proc.magnitude - 0.6613) < 5e-4, "Halving processing raises the ceiling to 0.66 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_ceiling_half_decel.magnitude - 0.4715) < 5e-4, "Halving the braking bound lowers the ceiling to 0.47 m/s.")
    check(v_ceiling_half_decel < v_clamp, "At half the braking bound the 0.5 m/s mode no longer fits.")
    check(abs(energy_nom.to(joule).magnitude - 13.5) < 1e-9, "Nominal translational energy must be 13.5 J.")
    check(abs(energy_clamp.to(joule).magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, "Restricted translational energy must be 1.5 J.")
    check(abs(a_tau.magnitude - 0.96) < 1e-9 and abs(two_a_d.magnitude - 1.35) < 1e-9, "Root operands must be 0.96 m/s and 1.35 m²/s².")
    check(abs((root_term - a_tau - v_ceiling).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The shown root minus a*tau must equal the ceiling.")
    check(
        abs(v_ceiling_check.magnitude - 0.5242) < 5e-4 and v_ceiling_check > v_clamp,
        "At 12 m/s² the ceiling (0.52 m/s) must still admit the 0.5 m/s mode.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    mass_str = fmt_qty(mass, unit=ureg.kg, precision=0)
    v_nom_str = fmt_velocity(v_nom, precision=2)
    v_clamp_str = fmt_velocity(v_clamp, precision=2)
    v_ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(v_ceiling, precision=2)
    v_ceiling_fast_proc_str = fmt_velocity(v_ceiling_fast_proc, precision=2)
    v_ceiling_half_decel_str = fmt_velocity(v_ceiling_half_decel, precision=2)
    processing_half_str = fmt_latency(processing / 2, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    deceleration_half_str = fmt_acceleration(deceleration / 2, precision=1)
    clearance_str = fmt_length(clearance, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    reserve_str = fmt_length(reserve, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    deceleration_str = fmt_acceleration(deceleration, precision=0)
    exposure_str = fmt_latency(exposure, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    processing_str = fmt_latency(processing, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    bus_str = fmt_latency(bus, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    onset_str = fmt_latency(onset, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    delay_str = fmt_latency(delay, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    blind_nom_str = fmt_length(blind_nom, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    brake_nom_str = fmt_length(brake_nom, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    stop_nom_str = fmt_length(stop_nom, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    deficit_str = fmt_length(deficit, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    stop_budget_str = fmt_length(stop_budget, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    blind_clamp_str = fmt_length(blind_clamp, unit=ureg.mm, precision=0)
    brake_clamp_str = fmt_length(brake_clamp, unit=ureg.mm, precision=1)
    stop_clamp_str = fmt_length(stop_clamp, unit=ureg.mm, precision=1)
    remaining_str = fmt_length(remaining, unit=ureg.mm, precision=1)
    energy_nom_str = fmt_energy(energy_nom, unit=joule, precision=1)
    energy_clamp_str = fmt_energy(energy_clamp, unit=joule, precision=1)
    energy_reduction_str = fmt_percent(energy_reduction, precision=1, style="prose")
    check_rate_str = fmt_frequency(check_rate, unit=ureg.kHz, precision=0)
    force_cap_str = fmt_force(force_cap, precision=0)
    temperature_trip_str = fmt_temperature(temperature_trip, precision=0)
    stall_timeout_str = fmt_latency(stall_timeout, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    bus_trip_str = fmt_voltage(bus_trip, precision=0)
    a_tau_str = fmt_velocity(a_tau, precision=2)
    two_a_d_str = fmt_qty(two_a_d, unit=ureg.meter**2 / ureg.second**2, precision=2)
    root_term_str = fmt_velocity(root_term, precision=2)
    deceleration_check_str = fmt_acceleration(deceleration_check, precision=0)
```

Because the carriage's momentum is already committed, the permission path must act before the carriage consumes its clearance. We test a candidate design using the constant-deceleration stopping formulation from @sec-body, evaluating hypothetical scenario inputs rather than measurements from a commissioned workcell.

::: {#nbk-frontier-packaging-delay-wall .callout-notebook title="The delay wall"}

**Problem**: The loaded carriage travels at `{python} PackagingCell.v_nom_str` toward a gate whose fixed stop line is `{python} PackagingCell.clearance_str` away when the hazardous closure begins, maintaining constant speed until braking begins. Can it stop short of the line, and if not, what is the fastest speed whose stop fits once a `{python} PackagingCell.reserve_str` reserve is held back?

**Variables**:

- Moving mass of carriage and loaded tray $m$ = `{python} PackagingCell.mass_str` and nominal speed $v$ = `{python} PackagingCell.v_nom_str` (Illustrative)
- Clearance `{python} PackagingCell.clearance_str`, less `{python} PackagingCell.reserve_str` reserved for uncertainty and residual clearance, leaves a stopping budget $d_{\text{budget}}$ = `{python} PackagingCell.stop_budget_str` (Illustrative)
- Braking lower bound $a_{\text{brake}}$ = `{python} PackagingCell.deceleration_str` after the delay (Illustrative; a bound to qualify under load, pad wear, and rail conditions, not a motor's peak rating)
- Delay from closure to full braking $\tau_{\text{delay}}$: `{python} PackagingCell.exposure_str` to a usable image, including frame phase and exposure, `{python} PackagingCell.processing_str` for transfer, inference, scheduling, and admission, `{python} PackagingCell.bus_str` for command delivery, and `{python} PackagingCell.onset_str` for brake buildup, in all `{python} PackagingCell.delay_str` (Illustrative upper bounds)

**Math**:

1. **Nominal stop** (@eq-body-stopping-distance, margins held in the reserve): $d_{\text{stop}} = v\tau_{\text{delay}} + v^2/2a_{\text{brake}}$ = `{python} PackagingCell.v_nom_str` $\times$ `{python} PackagingCell.delay_str` $+$ (`{python} PackagingCell.v_nom_str`)$^2/(2 \times$ `{python} PackagingCell.deceleration_str`) = `{python} PackagingCell.blind_nom_str` $+$ `{python} PackagingCell.brake_nom_str` = `{python} PackagingCell.stop_nom_str`, a deficit of `{python} PackagingCell.deficit_str`.
2. **Speed ceiling** (@eq-body-velocity-ceiling with $d_{\text{budget}}$ as the available distance): $a_{\text{brake}}\tau_{\text{delay}}$ = `{python} PackagingCell.a_tau_str` and $2a_{\text{brake}}d_{\text{budget}}$ = `{python} PackagingCell.two_a_d_str`, and the square root of (`{python} PackagingCell.a_tau_str`)$^2$ $+$ `{python} PackagingCell.two_a_d_str` is `{python} PackagingCell.root_term_str`. The positive root is $v_{\max}$ = `{python} PackagingCell.root_term_str` $-$ `{python} PackagingCell.a_tau_str` = `{python} PackagingCell.v_ceiling_str`.
3. **Candidate mode** at `{python} PackagingCell.v_clamp_str`, below the ceiling: `{python} PackagingCell.blind_clamp_str` of delay travel $+$ `{python} PackagingCell.brake_clamp_str` of braking = `{python} PackagingCell.stop_clamp_str`, leaving `{python} PackagingCell.remaining_str` before the stop line. Translational energy $E_k = mv^2/2$ falls from `{python} PackagingCell.energy_nom_str` to `{python} PackagingCell.energy_clamp_str`, a reduction of `{python} PackagingCell.energy_reduction_str`.

**Result**: At nominal speed the carriage reaches the gate before braking even begins. The budget admits at most `{python} PackagingCell.v_ceiling_str`, and the `{python} PackagingCell.v_clamp_str` candidate keeps more than the allocated reserve.

**Systems insight**: At these speeds delay travel, not braking, exhausts the clearance. The `{python} PackagingCell.delay_str` chain alone carries the nominal carriage `{python} PackagingCell.blind_nom_str`, farther than the stop line, so the condition $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$ of principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility} is met first by lowering speed or shortening the chain from closure to braking. The carriage's speed limit belongs to that whole chain, not to its brake alone.

:::

The slower mode is therefore worth qualifying. @Fig-17-packaging-cell partitions the physical plant, sensorimotor timing chain, and stopping envelopes across three aligned panels: panel (a) schematizes the physical track, mapping the carriage mass, carton insertion head, and drive motor against the optical gate stop line; panel (b) decomposes the cumulative `{python} PackagingCell.delay_str` pre-braking delay chain across image acquisition, transfer inference, bus transport, and brake onset; and panel (c) charts stopping distance on a millimeter axis, contrasting the nominal `{python} PackagingCell.v_nom_str` trajectory—which overruns the `{python} PackagingCell.clearance_str` stop line into the red hazard zone at `{python} PackagingCell.stop_nom_str`—against the clamped `{python} PackagingCell.v_clamp_str` mode that halts safely in `{python} PackagingCell.stop_clamp_str`, preserving the `{python} PackagingCell.reserve_str` stopping reserve.

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-packaging-figure
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PACKAGING CELL FIGURE LABELS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-17-packaging-cell (SVG labels are hand-typed).
# │ Goal:    Keep every delay and distance drawn in the figure equal to the
# │          PackagingCell values the prose prints.
# │ Show:    Nothing; the cell only guards the drawn labels.
# │ How:     Compare each drawn label (ms, mm, m/s) with its computed value.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class PackagingCellFigure:
    """Values drawn in fig17_packaging_cell.svg."""

    _P = PackagingCell
    _ms = lambda q: q.to(ureg.ms).magnitude
    _mm = lambda q: q.to(ureg.mm).magnitude
    _mps = lambda q: q.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude
    drawn = [
        ("image", 16.0, _ms(_P.exposure), 1e-9),
        ("transfer, inference, admission", 36.0, _ms(_P.processing), 1e-9),
        ("bus", 2.0, _ms(_P.bus), 1e-9),
        ("onset", 10.0, _ms(_P.onset), 1e-9),
        ("total delay", 64.0, _ms(_P.delay), 1e-9),
        ("clearance", 60.0, _mm(_P.clearance), 1e-9),
        ("reserve start", 45.0, _mm(_P.stop_budget), 1e-9),
        ("nominal speed", 1.5, _mps(_P.v_nom), 1e-9),
        ("restricted speed", 0.5, _mps(_P.v_clamp), 1e-9),
        ("nominal delay travel", 96.0, _mm(_P.blind_nom), 1e-9),
        ("nominal braking", 75.0, _mm(_P.brake_nom), 1e-9),
        ("nominal stop", 171.0, _mm(_P.stop_nom), 1e-9),
        ("restricted delay travel", 32.0, _mm(_P.blind_clamp), 1e-9),
        ("restricted stop", 40.3, _mm(_P.stop_clamp), 0.05),
        ("restricted spare", 19.7, _mm(_P.remaining), 0.05),
    ]
    for _name, _label, _value, _tol in drawn:
        check(abs(_label - _value) < _tol, f"packaging-cell figure label for {_name} is stale ({_label} vs {_value})")
```

::: {#fig-17-packaging-cell fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Three machine classes in one packaging cell**: (a) The carriage is the moving mass whose impact deforms carton and frame, the insertion head applies the contact force that can buckle a carton wall, and the drive dissipates heat that ages winding insulation. (b) The assumed delay chain from gate closure to full braking totals `{python} PackagingCell.delay_str`. (c) At `{python} PackagingCell.v_nom_str` the carriage travels `{python} PackagingCell.blind_nom_str` before braking begins and stops after `{python} PackagingCell.stop_nom_str`, far beyond the `{python} PackagingCell.clearance_str` stop line; at the restricted `{python} PackagingCell.v_clamp_str` it stops in `{python} PackagingCell.stop_clamp_str`, clear of the `{python} PackagingCell.reserve_str` reserve. All inputs are hypothetical design allocations, not measurements." fig-alt="Three panels. Panel a is a side-view schematic of a linear track with a drive box at the left end, a carriage carrying a carton, an insertion head pressing down on the carton, and a gate with a red dashed stop line at the right; labels name the drive as thermal dissipation with insulation aging, the carriage as moving mass whose impact deforms carton and frame, and the insertion head as contact force that buckles the carton wall. Panel b is a horizontal delay bar of four segments, image 16 ms, transfer inference and admission 36 ms, bus 2 ms, and brake onset 10 ms, totaling 64 ms from closure. Panel c shows two stopping-distance bars on a millimeter axis from 0 to 180 with a red dashed stop line at 60 mm and a hatched reserve band just before it. At 1.5 m/s the bar has 96 mm of delay travel and 75 mm of braking, reaching 171 mm, with the part beyond the stop line shaded red.
