:::

The quadratic root demonstrates how sensitive the velocity ceiling is to both computational latency and mechanical braking limits. Halving the processing allocation to `{python} PackagingCell.processing_half_str` raises the ceiling to `{python} PackagingCell.v_ceiling_fast_proc_str`; because reaction delay dominates stopping distance at high speed, faster admission buys the most velocity. Conversely, halving the qualified braking bound to `{python} PackagingCell.deceleration_half_str` lowers the ceiling to `{python} PackagingCell.v_ceiling_half_decel_str`, falling below the candidate `{python} PackagingCell.v_clamp_str` mode and eliminating it from consideration. The two premises play fundamentally different engineering roles. Shortening software latency creates an opportunity for higher throughput, whereas an unexpected braking shortfall invalidates the operational mode entirely. This asymmetry explains why engineers must qualify loaded deceleration empirically across worst-case operating conditions before commissioning the cell. The stopping equation defines the governing physical relationship, but only physical measurements on the assembled machine can establish that the latency budgets, deceleration bounds, and clearance reserves hold.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ This speed ceiling is the positive root first solved for the mobile base in @sec-body-dynamic-velocity-ceilings.
:::

The second law evaluates the empirical competence of the cell's learned proposers. This packaging cell deploys three distinct learned proposers: a vision model that infers container contents to propose carriage transit speeds, a multimodal network that estimates packaging cardboard thickness to propose insertion forces and dwell durations, and an electro-thermal estimator that proposes acceleration profiles to manage motor winding temperatures. In an embodied system, a proposer's actions directly alter what it observes next. Throttling carriage speed changes camera frame timing and optical motion blur; extending tool dwell changes the material deformation that subsequent thickness estimations read; and reshaping acceleration profiles changes the temperature trajectory measured by the thermal estimator. Empirical evidence of proposer competence therefore depends strictly on the state distribution sampled during closed-loop evaluation, raising the crucial question of whether that distribution matches the conditions admitted at runtime. Imposing a safety restriction after training creates an operational shift: if closed-loop evaluation sampled only the nominal transit speed of `{python} PackagingCell.v_nom_str`, clamping speed to `{python} PackagingCell.v_clamp_str` pushes the vision model into a regime of visual dynamics it never encountered during evaluation. A restriction designed to guarantee physical stopping distance simultaneously opens a regime without empirical evidence. The engineering team must either evaluate the policy under derated conditions prior to release or document the unverified regime as an open premise in the release sign-off.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ A policy whose actions choose its next observations is the endogenous covariate shift of @sec-data-covariate-shift; why evidence must come from the closed loop the machine will run is @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-dynamics.
:::

Closing this gap requires aligning the data-collection and evaluation campaign directly with the restricted operational envelope. Expert demonstrations must span the admitted transport velocities, insertion forces, and thermal regimes, preserving complete environmental metadata within the dataset provenance record. Once trained, the candidate proposer must undergo closed-loop trials on the physical cell to confirm that it successfully completes the packaging task under those conditions, including during interventions by the permission path. If the cell cannot maintain acceptable task performance within its physical bounds, engineers must revise the task specification, the proposer architecture, or the mechanical plant before re-evaluating the modified system. Calculating a defensible speed ceiling establishes physical safety, but only closed-loop verification demonstrates a viable packaging cell.

The third law places these proposed actions beneath an architectural authority split\index{Authority split} that the proposers cannot bypass, delay, or corrupt. The permission path prevents unverified neural proposals from reaching physical actuators directly. In this packaging workcell, an independent kinematic monitor runs at `{python} PackagingCell.check_rate_str`, evaluating optical encoders and rangefinder measurements to admit carriage motion commands only when real-time clearance supports the qualified stopping distance. The monitor's scheduling, sensory acquisition, and admission checks must execute within the `{python} PackagingCell.processing_str` processing budget; executing at a high loop frequency alone does not establish that end-to-end timing bound.

While the software kinematic check confines normal operation to the derated velocity mode, it does not carry the cell's formal protection claims. In an industrial deployment, harm-prevention claims rest upon hardware-certified drive safety functions codified under IEC 61800-5-2 [@iec61800part52] and mapped for warehouse automation in @tbl-12-certified-functions. The restricted transport mode maps to safely limited speed (SLS) on the carriage drive, an independent hardware function that continuously monitors motor velocity and triggers an emergency stop if the limit is exceeded. The emergency response executes as a ramp-monitored safe stop 1 (SS1) terminating in safe torque off (STO), with safe brake control (SBC) engaging mechanical holding brakes at rest. Each safety function requires a validated timing budget and an integrity metric. Under ISO 13849-1 [@iso13849part1], safety functions are classified by performance level (PL), which bounds their average probability of dangerous failure per hour according to the cell's risk assessment. The camera-triggered stop budgeted earlier represents an application-level proposal stop rather than a protective safety function. A safety-rated optical gate sensor feeding the drive's SS1 input directly replaces the frame-exposure and neural-inference allocations with its certified hardware response time, and that response time becomes $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ in the physical stopping model.

Physical safety limits must govern the insertion tool and actuator drives just as strictly as carriage motion. Configuring a mechanical force limiter to `{python} PackagingCell.force_cap_str` represents a nominal design setting rather than proof that every parcel resists crushing; empirical qualification must verify that peak transmitted forces—including dynamic overshoot during contact impact—remain below the yield strength of the weakest admitted carton and tab geometry. Similarly, setting a winding thermistor trip threshold at `{python} PackagingCell.temperature_trip_str` and a stall detection timeout of `{python} PackagingCell.stall_timeout_str` establishes basic supervisory cutoffs rather than a certified thermal envelope. Safe continuous operation depends on drive current profiles, winding resistance, heat capacity, cooling airflow, and sensor thermal lag. Because internal winding temperatures can surge before external housing sensors register the heat, engineers cannot validate a sustained duty cycle from trip thresholds alone without empirical thermal characterization.

High-rate deceleration also transfers mechanical kinetic energy back into the electrical drive system. During regenerative braking, the decelerating motor returns power to the inverter DC bus; a dynamic brake chopper and power resistor must absorb this energy before bus voltage exceeds the inverter trip threshold of `{python} PackagingCell.bus_trip_str`. The energy sink must accommodate repeated, cyclic stops throughout a shift rather than an isolated emergency event. Furthermore, regenerative braking requires an energized inverter stage throughout deceleration, whereas the carriage's electromechanical track brake relies on its own spring-actuated mechanism. Logic power hold-up alone supplies neither regenerative braking torque nor friction-brake clamping force. A thermal fault or electrical shutdown that cuts drive power disables regenerative braking, leaving deceleration entirely to the mechanical brake. System designers must ensure that safety-directed power cuts preserve a deterministic deceleration and holding response across every possible plant state.

The fourth law synthesizes these engineering decisions into a formal release argument. The cell's release manifest\index{Release manifest!packaging cell} must validate rangefinder coverage, gate clearance margins, braking deceleration, and sustained task throughput as an integrated whole. Equally important, the manifest explicitly records any claims that physical evidence cannot support. To verify tab latching integrity, the engineering team evaluates a vision model that inspects optical surface reflections for container tab engagement. Under industrial overhead lighting, specular reflections from tape and crinkled plastic packaging produce optical artifacts that mimic latch defects while masking genuine tab misalignments. Because the cell lacks an independent physical measurement—such as a tactile switch or a laser profile scanner—that distinguishes engaged tabs from misaligned flaps under glare, the sign-off claim lacks a qualified detector. Documenting this limitation as detectorless and unsupported in the residual-claims register\index{Residual-claims register!packaging cell} (@sec-frontier-residual-claims-register) is not a documentation failure, but an accurate statement of what the physical evidence justifies.

The stopping analysis therefore supports a *candidate restricted mode* for carriage transit at `{python} PackagingCell.v_clamp_str`, provided that the `{python} PackagingCell.delay_str` end-to-end latency, `{python} PackagingCell.deceleration_str` braking deceleration, `{python} PackagingCell.clearance_str` physical clearance, and uncertainty reserve are validated concurrently on the physical cell. Insertion forces and thermal duty cycles remain restricted until physical testing confirms material compressive limits, sensor thermal lag, and independent fault paths. Autonomous package sign-off is refused because optical glare obscures tab engagement from the vision system and the cell lacks an independent verification sensor. A qualified tactile or laser engagement sensor could support autonomous sign-off; mandatory downstream manual inspection instead supports a commercial deployment that makes no autonomous sign-off claim. An analytical throughput model cannot substitute for that empirical evidence.

By auditing the packaging cell across the four laws, systems engineers transform abstract safety objectives into an integrated sequence of concrete technical choices. Stopping mechanics identify a viable transport velocity envelope, which in turn defines the precise dynamic regime that data collection and closed-loop evaluation must cover. Runtime safety monitors enforce these dynamic limits in hardware and deterministic software, preventing policy proposals from breaching physical constraints. Finally, the release argument provides a transparent boundary between validated capabilities and unsupported claims, preventing catastrophic failures in edge cases. Physical AI systems succeed not by eliminating uncertainty through ever-larger models, but by bounding autonomy through verifiable physical laws.

This four-law audit protocol extends naturally beyond the mechanical archetypes of @sec-boundary-three-classes into fluid and chemical process systems, where the conserved irreversible quantity is mass flow or thermodynamic enthalpy rather than kinetic momentum. Consider a learned proposer that adjusts a dosing valve feeding a chemical reaction vessel. The first law asks: what mass of reagent has already been irrevocably committed? If a shutoff command experiences latency $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ at a volumetric flow rate $Q$, fluid continues to discharge, adding roughly $Q\tau_{\text{delay}}$ to the volume delivered while the valve physically closes—a direct fluidic analog of the mechanical stopping distance model. Stored thermodynamic and hydraulic energy similarly complicates fallback architectures. A pressurized accumulator, a cryogenic transfer line, or a heated pressure vessel retains stored energy even when electronic control power is severed. Much like balancing a bipedal humanoid, abruptly de-energizing the computational controller does not produce a safe state; the engineering design must name a qualified physical sink, such as a spring-loaded pressure relief bypass, to safely dissipate stored energy. The remaining three laws follow identically: policy evaluation must sample the throttled flow regimes that safety limits enforce; the permission path must guarantee valve closure within the allowable volumetric tolerance; and operational sign-off must ground all safety guarantees in measured valve slew rates and sensor response times.

::: {#chk-frontier-packaging-transfer .callout-checkpoint title="Transferring the four-law audit"}

The packaging cell demonstrates how the four-law audit organizes system design for an entirely novel machine, anchoring every operational claim to physical bounds and empirical measurements.

- [ ] **Speed-ceiling estimate**: Suppose physical load testing qualifies the carriage's braking bound at only `{python} PackagingCell.deceleration_check_str`, assuming the same `{python} PackagingCell.delay_str` total delay and `{python} PackagingCell.stop_budget_str` stopping budget. Estimate the updated velocity ceiling from the positive root of the stopping equation, and determine whether the candidate `{python} PackagingCell.v_clamp_str` mode still fits within this certified budget.
- [ ] **Machine classes**: For the carriage, the insertion head, and the linear drive motors, identify each component's physical machine class, the irreversible physical state transition it can produce, and the governing physical boundary.
- [ ] **Derated evaluation**: Explain why imposing a runtime velocity restriction after training induces an endogenous covariate shift for the vision proposer. What two engineering options can close this evaluation gap prior to operational sign-off?
- [ ] **Sign-off verdict**: What specific physical sensing evidence would be required to transition autonomous package sign-off from refused to supported, and why does simply expanding the training dataset with more glare-corrupted images fail to resolve the underlying detector deficiency?

:::
## The Epistemic Frontier {#sec-frontier-epistemic-limits}

A packaging cell's camera can confirm an arm's position and approve a transport motion without verifying that a hidden mechanical tab has engaged. Similarly, a warehouse robot's lidar and cameras can clear a navigation path across an aisle without determining whether the concrete floor provides sufficient traction to brake. These gaps represent fundamental epistemic limits: boundaries on what available sensory observations and analytical arguments can mathematically or physically justify. While additional training can improve a policy's action proposals, machine learning cannot manufacture unobserved physical reality. Systems engineers must identify whether validating the next operational claim demands broader training experience or a physical measurement absent from the existing sensor suite.

Consider an operational scenario where a pallet jack with a leaking hydraulic line crosses an active warehouse aisle, depositing a thin, transparent film of fluid onto polished concrete. The mobile manipulator's stopping budget assumes the floor provides sufficient surface friction for credible deceleration, which dry industrial concrete reliably supplies. Under an oil film, however, available traction collapses, yet neither standard navigation cameras nor time-of-flight lidars can distinguish the clear fluid from dry concrete. In this failure mode, the safety architecture operates exactly as specified: the software permission path clears every deadline, chunk leases expire predictably, and the actuator controller executes braking torque precisely on schedule. Nevertheless, the robot overruns the rack end and collides with the boundary. The failure stems not from software latency or actuator lag, but from an unmonitored premise: the local wheel-floor friction coefficient prior to braking. The stopping calculation evaluates this unobserved friction deficit:

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-oil-film
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE OIL FILM ON THE AISLE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-frontier-epistemic-limits (the premise behind the aisle
# │          speed), @sec-frontier-residual-claims-register (the register
# │          entries and @tbl-17-claims-register),
# │          @sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors (detection latency against the spare margin),
# │          @sec-frontier-fallacies-pitfalls (the vision-only pitfall).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that the 1.3 m/s normal mode always rested on a friction
# │          floor that no sensor on the machine reports.
# │ Show:    the friction the credible deceleration needs; the stop on a clear
# │          film against the clear distance; the inspected-floor ceiling and
# │          restricted mode; the zero-failure closure test; the time the spare
# │          margin buys; the film-detector range at a chosen latency; how much
# │          a time-form action deadline over-reserves against the distance form. The walking-person ceiling is Ch12's
# │          (@sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes) and is cited, not recomputed.
# │ How:     credible deceleration a = min(a_brake, mu g); the finished budget
# │          (jerk-limited S-curve stop, all three overheads) at the aisle speed,
# │          jerk bound = the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive
# │          limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix); its ceiling from
# │          calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity; zero-failure sample size.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics import calc_scurve_stop_time

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class OilFilm:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    g = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)  # category: measured (physical constant, standard gravity)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible deceleration, dry floor)
    mu_dry = AISLE.mu_dry  # category: illustrative (dry concrete)
    mu_insp = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative (inspected floor)
    mu_oil = AISLE.mu_oil_film  # category: illustrative (clear hydraulic film)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen (normal-mode aisle speed)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (pre-brake delay, excluding Delta_da)
    delta_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission  # category: illustrative (allocation of @sec-placement, not yet measured)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: derived (delta_loc + delta_margin + eps_track)
    v_h = AISLE.v_human_approach  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 walking speed)
    v_restricted = 1.0 * ureg.meter / ureg.second  # category: chosen (scenario assumption: restricted mode on inspected floors)
    p_miss_target = 0.001  # category: chosen (detector miss-rate bound for closure)
    n_contrast = 1000  # category: illustrative (a smaller zero-miss campaign, for contrast)
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen (one-sided confidence level)
    t_detect = 100 * ms  # category: chosen (film-detector sensing and inference latency, for the range condition)
    mu_check = 0.15  # category: illustrative (a measured floor, for the checkpoint estimate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    mu_min = (a_brake / g).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    a_dry = min(a_brake, mu_dry * g)
    a_insp = min(a_brake, mu_insp * g)
    a_oil = min(a_brake, mu_oil * g)
    # Jerk bound: the reference C2 polynomial's peak jerk at the drive limit; the
    # floor caps the deceleration, while the jerk bound belongs to the load.
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**3)

    # finished budget at the aisle speed: v tau + S-curve stop + overhead
    budget_aisle = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_dry, j_brake) + overhead).to(ureg.meter)
    spare_aisle = (d_clear - budget_aisle).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_latest = (spare_aisle / v_aisle).to(ms)
    reserve_da = (t_latest - delta_da).to(ms)  # timing allowance left after the Delta_da allocation
    stop_oil = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_oil, j_brake) + overhead).to(ureg.meter)
    # Visible terms of the finished budget (trapezoidal regime: v^2/2a + v a/2j, @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes)
    v_tau = (v_aisle * tau_delay).to(ureg.millimeter)
    brake_dry = (v_aisle**2 / (2 * a_dry)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    ramp_dry = (v_aisle * a_dry / (2 * j_brake)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    brake_oil = (v_aisle**2 / (2 * a_oil)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    ramp_oil = (v_aisle * a_oil / (2 * j_brake)).to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ceilings: the largest speed whose finished budget fits the clear distance
    margin_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
    ceiling_dry = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, tau_delay, a_dry, j_brake, margin_loc, AISLE.delta_margin)
    ceiling_insp = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, tau_delay, a_insp, j_brake, margin_loc, AISLE.delta_margin)

    # film detector: range needed so the dry-floor stop ends before the film's leading edge
    d_detect_min = (v_aisle * t_detect + budget_aisle).to(ureg.meter)

    # action deadline, time form vs distance form, for the S-curve stop at the aisle speed
    t_brake_aisle = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_aisle, a_dry, j_brake).to(ms)
    d_brake_aisle = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_dry, j_brake).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_brake_equiv = (d_brake_aisle / v_aisle).to(ms)  # time at the unchanged speed that the stop's distance represents
    t_overreserve = (t_brake_aisle - t_brake_equiv).to(ms)
    d_overreserve = (v_aisle * t_overreserve).to(ureg.millimeter)

    n_closure = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1.0 - p_miss_target, confidence=confidence)
    p_miss_contrast = 1.0 - calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_contrast, confidence=confidence)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, f"Friction floor should be 0.204, got {mu_min}.")
    check(a_dry == a_brake and mu_dry > mu_min, "On dry concrete the brakes, not friction, must bind.")
    check(mu_oil < mu_min and mu_insp < mu_min, "On the film and on an inspected floor friction must bind.")
    check(abs(a_insp.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2).magnitude - 1.1768) < 5e-4, f"Inspected-floor deceleration should be 1.18 m/s², got {a_insp}.")
    check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, f"Jerk bound should be the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak, got {j_brake}.")
    check(abs(budget_aisle.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 968.9925) < 5e-3, f"Budget at 1.3 m/s should be 968.99 mm, got {budget_aisle}.")
    check(abs(spare_aisle.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 131.0075) < 5e-3, f"Spare at 1.3 m/s should be 131.01 mm, got {spare_aisle}.")
    check(abs(t_latest.to(ms).magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, f"T_latest should be 100.8 ms, got {t_latest}.")
    check(reserve_da.magnitude > 0, "The Delta_da allocation must leave positive reserve at the aisle speed.")
    check(t_detect + delta_da > t_latest, "The chosen detector latency and the Delta_da allocation cannot both fit the allowance.")
    check(abs(ceiling_dry.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, f"Dry-floor ceiling should be 1.4367 m/s, got {ceiling_dry}.")
    check(
        abs(ceiling_insp.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, f"Inspected-floor ceiling should be 1.2309 m/s, got {ceiling_insp}."
    )
    check(
        v_restricted < ceiling_insp < v_aisle < ceiling_dry,
        "Restricted mode must sit under the inspected ceiling, and the aisle speed under the dry ceiling.",
    )
    check(abs(stop_oil.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 2.13) < 5e-3, f"Finished budget on the film should be 2.13 m, got {stop_oil}.")
    check(abs(a_oil.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2).magnitude - 0.49) < 5e-3, f"Film deceleration should be 0.49 m/s², got {a_oil}.")
    check(stop_oil > d_clear, f"On the film the incomplete budget from the aisle speed must already exceed the clear distance, got {stop_oil}.")
    check(n_closure == 2995, f"Zero-failure closure test should need 2,995 trials, got {n_closure}.")
    check(abs(d_detect_min.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 1098.9925) < 5e-3, f"Film-detector range should be 1.10 m, got {d_detect_min}.")
    check(abs(t_brake_aisle.magnitude - 931.25) < 1e-6, f"S-curve stop from 1.3 m/s should take 931.25 ms, got {t_brake_aisle}.")
    check(abs(d_brake_aisle.magnitude - 605.3125) < 1e-6, f"S-curve stop from 1.3 m/s should cover 605.31 mm, got {d_brake_aisle}.")
    check(abs(t_overreserve.magnitude - 465.625) < 1e-6, f"Time form over-reserves 465.6 ms, got {t_overreserve}.")
    check(d_overreserve > spare_aisle, "The time form's over-reservation exceeds the whole spare margin.")
    check(v_aisle > a_dry**2 / j_brake and v_aisle > a_oil**2 / j_brake, "Both stops must be in the trapezoidal regime for the shown terms.")
    check(
        abs((v_tau + brake_dry + ramp_dry + overhead - budget_aisle).to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6, "Shown dry terms must sum to the budget."
    )
    check(
        abs((v_tau + brake_oil + ramp_oil + overhead - stop_oil).to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6,
        "Shown film terms must sum to the film budget.",
    )
    check(mu_check * g < a_brake and mu_check > mu_insp, "The checkpoint floor must bind and lie above the inspected floor.")
    check(abs(p_miss_contrast - 0.002991) < 5e-7, f"1,000 zero-miss trials should bound the miss rate at 0.002991, got {p_miss_contrast}.")
    # margin_friction_floor_deceleration_knee.svg fig-alt hand-types 2 m/s², 0.204, 0.60, 0.12, 1.18, 0.05 and 0.49
    check(abs(a_brake.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Credible deceleration should be 2 m/s², got {a_brake}.")
    check(abs(mu_dry - 0.60) < 1e-9 and abs(mu_insp - 0.12) < 1e-9 and abs(mu_oil - 0.05) < 1e-9, "Floor coefficients should be 0.60, 0.12 and 0.05.")
    # margin_stop_time_overreserve_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 931.2, 465.6, 465.6 and 100.8 ms (guards above)

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(mu_min, precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_insp_str = fmt(mu_insp, precision=2)
    mu_oil_str = fmt(mu_oil, precision=2)
    a_insp_str = fmt_acceleration(a_insp, precision=2)
    a_oil_str = fmt_acceleration(a_oil, precision=2)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    budget_aisle_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_aisle_str = fmt_length(spare_aisle, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    t_latest_str = fmt_latency(t_latest, unit=ms, precision=1)
    delta_da_str = fmt_latency(delta_da, unit=ms, precision=1)
    reserve_da_str = fmt_latency(reserve_da, unit=ms, precision=1)
    stop_oil_str = fmt_length(stop_oil, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    ceiling_insp_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_insp, precision=2)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, precision=0)
    n_closure_str = fmt_int(n_closure, commas=True)
    n_contrast_str = fmt_int(n_contrast, commas=True)
    p_miss_contrast_str = fmt(p_miss_contrast, precision=6)
    p_miss_target_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_miss_target, precision=1, style="prose")
    p_miss_target_sym_str = fmt_percent(p_miss_target, precision=1, style="symbol")
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, style="prose")
    confidence_sym_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, style="symbol")
    v_h_str = fmt_velocity(v_h, precision=1)
    t_detect_str = fmt_latency(t_detect, unit=ms, precision=0)
    d_detect_min_str = fmt_length(d_detect_min, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    t_brake_aisle_str = fmt_latency(t_brake_aisle, unit=ms, precision=1)
    t_brake_equiv_str = fmt_latency(t_brake_equiv, unit=ms, precision=1)
    t_overreserve_str = fmt_latency(t_overreserve, unit=ms, precision=1)
    d_overreserve_str = fmt_length(d_overreserve, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    g_str = fmt_acceleration(g, precision=2)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=ms, precision=1)
    j_brake_str = fmt_qty(j_brake, unit=ureg.meter / ureg.second**3, precision=2)
    overhead_str = fmt_length(overhead, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=0)
    v_tau_str = fmt_length(v_tau, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    brake_dry_str = fmt_length(brake_dry, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    ramp_dry_str = fmt_length(ramp_dry, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    brake_oil_str = fmt_length(brake_oil, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    ramp_oil_str = fmt_length(ramp_oil, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    mu_check_str = fmt(mu_check, precision=2)
```

The release decision in @sec-release-safety-cases-claims already encountered this premise: claim C3 (braking traction) was refused on this book's own evidence and deferred to this chapter as an unresolved premise. A machine's credible deceleration is governed by whichever is smaller—actuator braking capacity or tire-floor contact traction:[^fn-amontons-coulomb-friction]
$$a = \min(a_{\text{brake}}, \mu g).$$ {#eq-frontier-credible-deceleration}
This friction term establishes the physical ceiling on wheel-ground force illustrated in @fig-02-braking-fbd. On an oily surface, interface friction—not motor torque—becomes the binding constraint.

::: {#nbk-frontier-friction-floor .callout-notebook title="The friction floor"}

**Problem**: A clear hydraulic film lies across the aisle. Does the finished dry-floor stop from the candidate `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str` aisle speed still fit the rack end's `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance?

**Variables**:

- Credible deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$ = `{python} OilFilm.a_brake_str` (Illustrative, @sec-body-kinetic-momentum) and $g$ = `{python} OilFilm.g_str` (Measured constant)
- Floor friction $\mu$ = `{python} OilFilm.mu_dry_str` on dry industrial concrete and `{python} OilFilm.mu_oil_str` under the film (both Illustrative; see the Reader Guide)
- Aisle speed $v$ = `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str` (Chosen) and clear distance $D_{\text{clear}}$ = `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` (Illustrative)
- Known-component terms of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget: pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ = `{python} OilFilm.tau_delay_str`, jerk bound $j_{\max}$ = `{python} OilFilm.j_brake_str`, and fixed overheads of `{python} OilFilm.overhead_str` (all Derived)

**Math**:

1. **Friction floor** (@eq-frontier-credible-deceleration): The brake binds only while $\mu \ge a_{\text{brake}}/g$ = `{python} OilFilm.a_brake_str` $/$ `{python} OilFilm.g_str` = `{python} OilFilm.mu_min_str`. Dry concrete clears it; the film does not, so $a = \mu g$ = `{python} OilFilm.mu_oil_str` $\times$ `{python} OilFilm.g_str` = `{python} OilFilm.a_oil_str`.
2. **Dry-floor budget**: Delay travel $v\tau_{\text{delay}}$ $+$ braking $v^2/2a$ $+$ jerk-ramp travel $va/2j_{\max}$ $+$ overheads = `{python} OilFilm.v_tau_str` $+$ `{python} OilFilm.brake_dry_str` $+$ `{python} OilFilm.ramp_dry_str` $+$ `{python} OilFilm.overhead_str` = `{python} OilFilm.budget_aisle_str`.
3. **Film budget**: The same terms at $a$ = `{python} OilFilm.a_oil_str` give `{python} OilFilm.v_tau_str` $+$ `{python} OilFilm.brake_oil_str` $+$ `{python} OilFilm.ramp_oil_str` $+$ `{python} OilFilm.overhead_str` = `{python} OilFilm.stop_oil_str`.

**Result**: On the film the stop grows from `{python} OilFilm.budget_aisle_str` to `{python} OilFilm.stop_oil_str`, far past the `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance, and this budget still omits the dispatch-to-admission interval.

**Systems insight**: Below $\mu$ = `{python} OilFilm.mu_min_str` the floor, not the brake or the timing, sets the deceleration, and the braking term grows as $1/\mu$. Faster admission can recover only the `{python} OilFilm.v_tau_str` of delay travel, so no improvement in the permission path restores the dry-floor mode on the film. Only a restriction or a measurement at the tire-floor interface can keep $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$.

:::

The calculation omits the dispatch-to-admission interval, which @sec-placement allocates but no loaded measurement yet confirms; that interval adds travel and reduces every derived speed ceiling. Even this incomplete budget already excludes the film.

[^fn-amontons-coulomb-friction]: **Amontons-Coulomb Friction**\index{Friction coefficient!Amontons-Coulomb}: The classical laws of sliding friction make the friction force proportional to the normal load and independent of the apparent contact area, which is what lets a single coefficient $\mu$ describe a contact. @bowden1950friction traced the law to the small true area of contact, whose shear strength sets $\mu$, and showed that a lubricant film only molecules thick can lower it several-fold. The coefficient therefore belongs to the pair of surfaces and whatever lies between them, not to the floor alone, and the braking premise needs a measurement at the tire-floor interface that no camera viewing the floor supplies.

The friction premise did not emerge merely when fluid leaked onto the concrete. The candidate normal operating mode of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes implicitly assumed that unmeasured friction floor across every aisle, dry or wet. These evidence streams are orthogonal: resolving software timing uncertainties does not guarantee physical traction, and confirming traction does not eliminate scheduling delays.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_friction_floor_deceleration_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Plot of credible deceleration against floor friction coefficient. An amber line rises from the origin to 2 meters per second squared at a dashed vertical line marked μ 0.204, then runs flat. The region left of the dashed line is shaded and labeled floor binds; the flat part is labeled brake binds. A dot on the flat part marks dry μ 0.60. On the rising part, an amber dot marks the inspected floor, μ 0.12, at 1.18, and a red dot marks the film, μ 0.05, at 0.49."}

*Below $\mu$ = `{python} OilFilm.mu_min_str`, the floor, not the brake, sets the deceleration.*
:::

The oil film stresses the safety architecture directly at the boundary between physical measurement and software permission. An independent safety enforcer can reject action proposals that violate a validated stopping envelope, but accelerating enforcer execution cannot overcome an unverified friction coefficient. The drive electronics continue to regulate motor current and commanded torque with millisecond precision (@sec-body-electrical-time-constants), yet that torque translates into deceleration solely through tire-floor contact mechanics. Ensuring safety requires either a verified physical sensor at the interface or an enforceable operational restriction rather than another layer of neural inference.

The manipulator arm's contact limit at the door latch exposes an identical structural vulnerability: safety depends on a latch that holds under any force below the arm's contact ceiling. Yet mechanical wear, material fatigue, or chemical corrosion can silently reduce the latch's yield force below that threshold, even while joint torque sensors report nominal readings identical to those against a pristine strike plate. A wrist force-torque sensor whose zero-point calibration has drifted creates the same hazard for every contact threshold that depends on its signal (@sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment).

In each scenario, a machine can depart from its safe operating envelope while internal telemetry remains completely nominal. Successful empirical runs under nominal conditions provide no safety guarantee once an underlying physical premise fails. A rigorous safety case must explicitly catalog each unobserved premise, restrict operational authority while that premise remains unverified, and define the empirical evidence required to close it. For every open entry, systems discipline requires determining what the machine can physically measure, what actuator limits can still prevent, and which operational claims must remain refused.

### What the release claim rests on {#sec-frontier-method-limits}

A mobile manipulator's release claim forms a chain of dependent arguments determined by operational hazards and selected mitigations (@sec-boundary-machine-model). The complete safety case must establish the operational design domain, measured actuator performance, stopping bounds, component interface contracts, and independent permission filtering for learned proposals. Hazards managed by runtime detection demand verified detector coverage and bounded monitoring latency. Conversely, hazards managed through passive compliance or operational constraints require empirical evidence that those safeguards hold across declared payloads, component wear, and environmental exposures. Extensive testing of one link cannot compensate for an unsupported premise in another.[^fn-popper-falsification-asymmetry]

[^fn-popper-falsification-asymmetry]: **Popperian Falsification**\index{Falsification!Popperian induction}: The asymmetry holds for universal hypotheses [@popper1959logic]. No finite run of safe stops proves that every aisle floor supplies the friction floor, and one measured film below it refutes that premise. A rate claim, such as a hazard rate per hour, is neither refuted by one incident nor proved by many incident-free hours, so it is bounded statistically and revised as exposure accumulates. This chapter therefore holds deterministic premises in register entries and rate claims in confidence bounds.

Each premise in a safety case carries one of five formal statuses defined in the Reader Guide: established by measurement or derivation, assumed, decided by accountable judgment, unsupported, or outside the threat model. The envelope trichotomy (\ref{dfn-release-envelope-trichotomy}) classifies an actively monitored runtime condition as known-true, known-false, or unknown. Crucially, the unobserved premises bounding physical AI systems cannot be evaluated by active runtime monitors; internal telemetry cannot label them known-true. Consequently, release certification must either validate and maintain these premises through external physical evidence or constrain operational authority accordingly. For the mobile base, stopping-distance guarantees rest on an assumed wheel-floor friction coefficient that cannot be observed prior to braking. For the manipulator arm, contact safety assumes a minimum yield strength for the door latch and manipulated objects—a threshold established by engineering judgment rather than real-time measurement. For the wrist transducer, force-limiting safety functions assume zero-point calibration stability, a condition internal telemetry cannot verify without an unloaded physical tare. Documenting these premises explicitly does not weaken a release case; rather, it delineates the precise physical boundary where system guarantees hold and beyond which operational authority must be revoked.

Separating empirical measurement from accountable judgment is fundamental to systems engineering discipline. Rigorous testing and statistical characterization can estimate physical exposure, quantify sensor noise, and bound parametric uncertainty, but empirical data cannot select an acceptable residual risk\index{Residual risk} or dictate which individuals in an operating facility must bear that risk. Those choices represent accountable engineering decisions that must be documented as explicit judgments rather than disguised as objective empirical facts. Similarly, the threat model\index{Threat model} in @sec-verification circumscribes the operational validity of the safety record. Empirical evaluations across nominal fleet workflows and random component faults provide zero evidence regarding intentional adversarial attacks. A test campaign demonstrating that a vision pipeline tolerates lens flare, sensor noise, and partial occlusions provides no statistical support for claims regarding resilience against adversarial optical projections, policy weight tampering, or intentional denial-of-service disruptions across the internal communication bus.

#### Conditional shield dilution and common-cause bounds {#sec-frontier-shield-dilution}

Among the links in the safety chain, system designers most frequently overestimate the permission path. While @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention established deterministic guarantees for each command evaluated by a safety shield, translating those per-command filtering guarantees into system-level hazard-rate claims requires careful statistical accounting. A pervasive misconception in physical AI is that adding a safety shield renders the upstream policy's proposal error rate irrelevant. In reality, a shield acts as a conditional filter: the resulting operational hazard rate depends directly on how often the neural policy proposes hazardous actions, the shield's conditional interception probability, and failures that occur entirely outside the shield's sensing domain. The following calculation quantifies these interactions in an illustrative deployment:

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-architectural-shield-dilution
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_sci, fmt, fmt_int, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_empirical_testing_exposure,
    calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate,
    calc_zero_failure_sample_size,
)

# ┌── 1. INPUT (Illustrative target and distinct evidence records) ────
p_target = 1.0e-9  # category: illustrative (system incidents/hour target, not a statutory rate)
confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen (one-sided confidence level)
alpha = 1.0 - confidence  # category: derived (significance level)

fleet_units = 100  # category: illustrative (fleet size)
t_cycle_days = 90.0  # category: illustrative (release cycle length)
hours_per_day = 24.0  # category: illustrative (continuous operation)

c_shield_assumed = 0.9999  # category: illustrative (class-specific interception coverage)
p_hw_assumed = 0.0  # category: illustrative (hardware and common-cause residual set to zero)
proposal_events_hypothetical = 0  # category: illustrative (adjudicated counterfactual-oracle proposal log)

# ┌── 2. COMPUTE (Proposal-log bound and shield decomposition) ────────
# The adjudicated proposal log covers one full cycle of the fleet.
t_cycle_hours = t_cycle_days * hours_per_day
proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical = fleet_units * t_cycle_hours
# Zero hazardous proposals bound the proposal rate (one-sided Poisson).
p_proposal_upper_hypothetical = -math.log(alpha) / proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical

# Conditional design arithmetic: the proposal-rate bound the target would require
# at the assumed class-specific interception coverage, and the exposure to show it.
p_proposal_limit = (p_target - p_hw_assumed) / (1.0 - c_shield_assumed)
n_brain_hours = calc_empirical_testing_exposure(p_proposal_limit, confidence=confidence)
t_test_days = n_brain_hours.magnitude / (fleet_units * hours_per_day)
p_system_conditional = calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate(
    p_proposal_upper_hypothetical / ureg.hour, c_shield_assumed, p_hw_assumed / ureg.hour
).magnitude
c_required_cycle = 1.0 - (p_target - p_hw_assumed) / p_proposal_upper_hypothetical
test_overrun_days = t_test_days - t_cycle_days

# Coverage is itself a claim: zero misses in n seeded hazardous proposals of
# the class bound c_h from below. A joint statement from two one-sided bounds
# needs each at 1 - alpha/2 (Bonferroni), which moves both numbers.
n_coverage = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(c_shield_assumed, confidence=confidence)
confidence_split = 1.0 - alpha / 2.0
n_coverage_joint = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(c_shield_assumed, confidence=confidence_split)
p_proposal_upper_joint = -math.log(alpha / 2.0) / proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical
p_system_joint = calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate(p_proposal_upper_joint / ureg.hour, c_shield_assumed, p_hw_assumed / ureg.hour).magnitude

# ┌── 3. GUARDS (Statistical bounds & invariance checks) ──────────────
check(abs(proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical - 216000.0) < 1.0, f"Unexpected proposal-log hours: {proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical}")
check(abs(p_proposal_upper_hypothetical - 1.3869e-5) < 1e-8, f"Unexpected proposal bound: {p_proposal_upper_hypothetical}")
check(proposal_events_hypothetical == 0, "Proposal scenario requires zero events")
check(abs(p_proposal_limit - 1.0e-5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected proposal limit: {p_proposal_limit}")
check(abs(n_brain_hours.magnitude - 299573.0) < 100.0, f"Unexpected brain exposure: {n_brain_hours}")
check(abs(t_test_days - 124.8) < 1.0, f"Unexpected test days: {t_test_days}")
check(abs(p_system_conditional - 1.386913e-9) < 1e-12, f"Unexpected conditional residual: {p_system_conditional}")
check(abs(c_required_cycle - 0.9999278974) < 1e-8, f"Unexpected required coverage: {c_required_cycle}")
check(test_overrun_days > 34.0, f"Unexpected 90-day overrun: {test_overrun_days}")
check(n_coverage == 29956, f"Coverage campaign at 95 percent should be 29,956 trials, got {n_coverage}")
check(n_coverage_joint == 36887, f"Coverage campaign at 97.5 percent should be 36,887 trials, got {n_coverage_joint}")
check(abs(p_proposal_upper_joint - 1.7078e-5) < 1e-8, f"Unexpected 97.5 percent proposal bound: {p_proposal_upper_joint}")
check(abs(p_system_joint - 1.7078e-9) < 1e-12, f"Unexpected joint residual: {p_system_joint}")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Canonical formatting) ────────────────────────────────
class ArchitecturalShieldDilution:
    n_proposal_sci_str = fmt_sci(proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical, precision=2)
    p_proposal_upper_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_proposal_upper_hypothetical, precision=3)

    p_brain_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_proposal_limit, precision=0)
    n_brain_sci_str = fmt_sci(n_brain_hours.magnitude, precision=2)
    t_test_days_str = fmt(t_test_days, precision=1)
    p_system_conditional_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_system_conditional, precision=3)
    c_required_str = fmt(c_required_cycle, precision=7)
    test_overrun_days_str = fmt(test_overrun_days, precision=1)
    n_coverage_str = fmt_int(n_coverage, commas=True)
    n_coverage_joint_str = fmt_int(n_coverage_joint, commas=True)
    p_proposal_upper_joint_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_proposal_upper_joint, precision=3)
    p_system_joint_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_system_joint, precision=3)
    # Operands shown in the notebook's Math lines
    fleet_units_str = fmt_int(fleet_units)
    t_cycle_days_str = fmt(t_cycle_days, precision=0)
    hours_per_day_str = fmt(hours_per_day, precision=0)
    neg_ln_alpha_str = fmt(-math.log(alpha), precision=3)
    neg_ln_alpha_half_str = fmt(-math.log(alpha / 2.0), precision=3)
    c_shield_str = fmt(c_shield_assumed, precision=4)
    one_minus_c_sci_str = fmt_sci(1.0 - c_shield_assumed, precision=0)
    p_target_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_target, precision=0)
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, style="prose")
    confidence_split_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence_split, precision=1, style="prose")
    alpha_str = fmt(alpha, precision=2)
```

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The exposure wall is defined in @sec-evaluation-limits, from the zero-failure rule of three of @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival.
:::

Consider an illustrative system target of `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_target_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$. This metric originates in civil aviation certification, where catastrophic failure conditions must be demonstrated to be "extremely improbable," on the order of $10^{-9}$ per flight hour[^fn-extremely-improbable-band] [@faa1988ac251309]. While no industrial robotics standard mandates this specific threshold, examining it illustrates the severe statistical burdens imposed by borrowed safety targets. Furthermore, as established by the exposure wall, physical operating hours alone cannot feasibly certify failure rates of this magnitude.[^fn-pooling-evidence-updates] The critical engineering question is what safety margin a runtime shield genuinely contributes against that target, and what supporting evidence its own operation demands.

[^fn-extremely-improbable-band]: **Extremely Improbable Band**\index{Extremely improbable!failure condition}: The advisory circular offers its probability bands as aids to engineering judgment, expressed per flight hour of a mean-duration flight and applied to each failure condition separately, and it grounds such criteria in historical accident data [@faa1988ac251309]. The $10^{-9}$ figure is therefore one catastrophic condition's share of a certified design's risk, not a rate for a whole aircraft, let alone for another kind of machine. Borrowing the number without the argument that set its share borrows a figure without its budget.

[^fn-pooling-evidence-updates]: **Pooling Evidence Across Updates**\index{Exposure wall!retraining reset}: An updated model may alter the proposal distribution. Earlier data can be pooled only with a justified configuration-equivalence and exposure argument; an update does not automatically erase every observation. The exposure wall's constant-rate model also requires a defensible treatment of shared fleet conditions and correlated faults.

A safety shield argument is inherently *conditional*. Observed incident rates across an operating fleet already incorporate the protective interventions of runtime filters and human supervisors. Multiplying an observed incident rate by a shield's interception factor double-counts that protection. For a defined hazard class $h$, let $\lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}$ denote the arrival rate of unshielded, hazardous action proposals emitted by the policy prior to the permission layer, and let $c_h = P(\mathrm{intercept}\mid\mathrm{hazardous\ proposal},h)$ represent the verified interception coverage for that specific hazard class. Accounting for an independently bounded hardware fault and common-cause arrival rate $\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$, the true conditional hazard rate is governed by @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard:
$$\lambda_{\mathrm{system},h} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}(1-c_h)+\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$$ {#eq-frontier-shielded-hazard}
Here, $\lambda_{\mathrm{system},h}$, $\lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}$, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$ represent rates per operating hour, while $c_h$ is a unitless conditional probability. The asymptotic limits clarify the shield's operational capability. With perfect detection and interception ($c_h = 1$), the system hazard rate reduces to the hardware and common-cause floor $\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$. Conversely, if the shield possesses zero coverage ($c_h = 0$), the raw proposal hazard rate passes unattenuated to the actuators. This relation translates the runtime assurance architecture of @sec-enforcement—which pairs an unverified primary controller with a verified safety filter [@sha2001using; @hsu2024safetyfilter]—into operational reliability metrics.

Evaluating @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard requires four foundational premises. The first is a verified **counterfactual oracle**\index{Counterfactual oracle!definition}—an objective evaluation harness that determines whether an unshielded action proposal would have caused a safety violation; without this oracle, the raw proposal error rate $\lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}$ cannot be measured. The remaining requirements comprise timely hazard detection, adequate actuator braking authority, and a rigorous accounting of correlated failures\index{Common-cause failure!shield coverage}. Designers frequently neglect this final common-cause term. Release claim C5 required empirical validation rather than theoretical assumption because distinct implementations of identical specifications exhibit correlated failures far more frequently than statistical independence assumes (@sec-release-contextual-assumptions). The product $\lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}(1-c_h)$ treats an enforcer miss as independent of the environmental conditions that triggered the hazardous proposal. Yet an occluded camera frame that induces a bad trajectory proposal in the neural policy can simultaneously corrupt the state estimator in the safety shield. Such common-cause degradation does not simply add an independent background term to $\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$; it systematically depresses $c_h$ precisely in the operational states where errors occur. Consequently, interception coverage $c_h$ must be evaluated over the empirical distribution of policy failures rather than an idealized set of synthetic test cases. The mathematical formulation provides no safety credit for unobserved hazards such as oil films or fatigue-weakened latches, and release approval cannot proceed until each premise is empirically supported.

Bounding the system hazard rate requires bounding the raw proposal rate $\lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}$ using an adjudicated execution log before crediting shield attenuation. Under a stationary Poisson arrival model with zero observed hazardous proposals, this upper bound follows the rule of three [@hanley1983nothing] introduced in @sec-evaluation-closed-loop-survival (@eq-eval-rule-of-three), substituting proposal operating hours for discrete trials. For an adjudicated evaluation log spanning $T$ operating hours at significance level $\alpha$, the one-sided upper confidence bound is $-\ln\alpha/T$, which evaluates to approximately $3/T$ at `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.confidence_pct_str` confidence:

::: {#nbk-frontier-fleet-exposure-and-shielded-decomposition .callout-notebook title="The coverage bill"}

**Problem**: In an illustrative scenario, a fleet keeps a fully adjudicated proposal log for one release cycle, judged by a validated counterfactual oracle, and the log records no hazardous proposal. If a named shield's interception coverage for that hazard class were independently established, would the modeled residual of @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard meet the system target, and what evidence would it take to show that it does?

**Variables**:

- System target $\lambda_{\text{target}}$ = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_target_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$ (Illustrative)
- Proposal log $T$ = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.fleet_units_str` units $\times$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.t_cycle_days_str` days $\times$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.hours_per_day_str` h = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_proposal_sci_str` proposal-hours with zero hazardous proposals (Illustrative)
- Class-specific coverage $c_h$ = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.c_shield_str` and $\lambda_{\text{other}}$ = 0 (Illustrative; the hardware and common-cause term is set to zero for this calculation)
- Confidence `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.confidence_pct_str`, significance $\alpha$ = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.alpha_str` (Chosen)

**Math**:

1. **Proposal bound** (rule of three with hours in place of trials): $-\ln\alpha / T$ = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.neg_ln_alpha_str` $/$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_proposal_sci_str` h = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_proposal_upper_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$.
2. **Residual**: `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_proposal_upper_sci_str` $\times$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.one_minus_c_sci_str` $+$ 0 = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_system_conditional_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$, **above** the target. Meeting it at this bound needs $c_h \ge 1 -$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_target_sci_str` $/$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_proposal_upper_sci_str` = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.c_required_str`.
3. **Proposal evidence at the assumed coverage**: The bound must fall to `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_target_sci_str` $/$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.one_minus_c_sci_str` = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_brain_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$, which takes `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.neg_ln_alpha_str` $/$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_brain_sci_str` = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_brain_sci_str` proposal-hours, or `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.t_test_days_str` days for the fleet, `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.test_overrun_days_str` days beyond the cycle.
4. **Coverage evidence**: Bounding $c_h$ itself takes $\ln$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.alpha_str` $/ \ln$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.c_shield_str` = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_coverage_str` seeded hazardous proposals of that class with no miss, drawn from the states in which the policy errs.
5. **Joint confidence**: The probability that at least one of two bounds fails is at most the sum of their failure probabilities, so a joint `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.confidence_pct_str` statement needs each bound at `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.confidence_split_pct_str` (the Bonferroni split). The proposal bound becomes `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.neg_ln_alpha_half_str` $/$ `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_proposal_sci_str` h = `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_proposal_upper_joint_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$, the coverage campaign `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_coverage_joint_str` trials, and the residual `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_system_joint_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$.

**Result**: The modeled residual misses the target even with the common-cause term set to zero. Supporting the claim takes both a proposal log longer than the release cycle and tens of thousands of seeded interceptions, and the confidence of the combined claim must be budgeted across them.

**Systems insight**: A shield changes the system claim only for hazard classes it can detect and intercept in time. Proposal frequency, conditional interception coverage, hardware faults, and common-cause failures need separate evidence. Oil or material failure outside the shield's sensing coverage stays in the residual-claims register.

:::

This analysis applies the exposure model established in @sec-evaluation-trial-limits alongside the safety filter from @sec-enforcement without fabricating empirical evidence for either. Formal verification carries the identical burden of explicit scoping: any mathematical certificate applies solely to the declared kinematic model, sensory observations, disturbance bounds, and timing guarantees (@sec-verification-formal-limits). Whenever a physical premise lacks empirical proof, the release argument must substitute an operational restriction assigned to an accountable owner.

### A residual-claims register {#sec-frontier-residual-claims-register}

Refusing claim C3 in the safety case did not eliminate the underlying friction premise. The **residual-claims register**\index{Residual-claims register!definition}\index{Contracts!residual claims} serves as the fifteenth and concluding document in the systems record chain (@sec-appendix-systems-record-register). Consuming the upstream release manifest from @sec-release-manifest, the register tethers every unresolved physical premise directly to an operational restriction. Without this explicit linkage, a subsequent model update could restore an unauthorized operating mode while leaving its invalid physical premise entirely unaddressed.

Each register entry specifies four required elements: the missing physical observable, the active containment mechanism or operational restriction, the accountable owner, and a predeclared empirical closure test. These components give principle \ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority} direct operational force. Unlike a conventional defect log or issue tracker, the register is a machine-readable deployment record. Its parameters govern runtime enforcer bounds, and its standing stipulations bind facility operations. Operational authority remains strictly derated until rigorous empirical evidence satisfies the designated closure test; documenting an engineering caveat or deferring an open premise to a future release without restricting speed or narrowing the operational design domain provides zero physical protection.

Engineers must define each **missing observable**\index{Missing observable!definition} through concrete physical quantities rather than modeling abstractions. Labeling an anomaly as an "out-of-distribution latent state" offers no guidance on what physical transducer must measure it or when an enforcer must intervene. By contrast, identifying an unmeasured friction coefficient or latch yield force provides immediate actionable clarity. A physical definition allows the engineering team to evaluate the trade-offs among adding physical sensors, enforcing passive mechanical boundaries, or narrowing the operational design domain—and establishes precisely what evidence is required to retire the restriction.

The undetected oil film establishes the first register entry for the mobile manipulator. The foundational premise asserts that all aisle floors provide a friction coefficient of at least $\mu \ge$ `{python} OilFilm.mu_min_str`, the threshold required to achieve credible deceleration. The missing observable is the local friction coefficient beneath a clear fluid film, which neither onboard cameras nor lidars can distinguish from clean concrete. Because a stopping trajectory calibrated for dry concrete overruns the available clearance on an oily surface, the normal velocity limit can be justified only across surfaces where friction is verified or actively controlled.

An unresolved premise mandates an immediate **operational response**\index{Operational response!definition}. For warehouse aisles, release certification can authorize a derated operational speed of `{python} OilFilm.v_restricted_str` on designated transit paths maintained under a strict facility inspection protocol. In this restricted-service regime, qualified surface scrubbing, spill isolation, and controlled access ensure a minimum friction coefficient of $\mu \ge$ `{python} OilFilm.mu_insp_str`. This floor yields a credible deceleration of `{python} OilFilm.a_insp_str` and a known-component velocity ceiling of `{python} OilFilm.ceiling_insp_str`, corresponding to the dashed envelope in @fig-12-stopping-vs-speed. This floor represents an illustrative baseline chosen below dry concrete to tolerate minor surface contamination; a production deployment must derive this value from empirical friction surveys across the designated routes. In the illustrative project records, restricted-mode operation remains provisional until the full timing budget—including dispatch-to-admission latency and required reserves—is empirically verified. Routes not covered by the facility inspection regime are strictly excluded from automated navigation.

Restricted operations require an accountable owner capable of maintaining the validity of the underlying physical assumptions. Facility operations owns this entry through its maintenance and spill-response procedures along material-handling routes, specifying inspection cadences and defining environmental conditions that trigger operational shutdown. While the cryptographically signed speed ceiling in the onboard permission path enforces motion constraints, a software speed setting alone cannot guarantee surface friction.

Every register entry must specify a rigorous **closure test**\index{Closure test!definition} formulated prior to data collection. To detect surface films online, the closure test must qualify an independent physical sensing modality, since standard visual cameras and lidars cannot resolve clear fluids in this environment. Alternatively, modified floor coatings or active physical containment could support a revised safety claim through separate structural evidence. One proposed closure campaign evaluates an optical film detector, requiring a bounded miss rate of at most `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_pct_str` demonstrated through `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` zero-failure trials on seeded fluid films (@sec-evaluation-trial-limits); until the sensor passes this qualification, the operational speed derating remains mandatory. Smaller evaluation campaigns fail to provide adequate statistical confidence: achieving zero misses across `{python} OilFilm.n_contrast_str` independent trials bounds the miss probability only at `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_contrast_str` at `{python} OilFilm.confidence_pct_str` confidence. Furthermore, the detector must provide sufficient forward sensing range so that sensing latency, permission processing, and physical braking complete prior to reaching the contaminant. Forward range, inference latency, false-positive rates, and post-detection friction assumptions must all be specified in advance. Reactive wheel-slip reflexes can limit subsequent acceleration but cannot guarantee stopping distance before the drive wheels strike the fluid.

While the target miss rate of `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_pct_str` is chosen illustratively here, a production deployment must formally derive it. The detector operates within the conditional shield framework of @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard, where fluid film encounters replace hazardous action proposals. If films occur along transit routes at an arrival rate $\lambda_{\text{film}}$ and facility engineering allocates a hazard budget $\lambda_{\text{alloc}}$ to this failure mode, the detector must satisfy $\lambda_{\text{film}}\,p_{\text{miss}} \le \lambda_{\text{alloc}}$. Defining the risk allocation $\lambda_{\text{alloc}}$ is an accountable engineering judgment, whereas estimating the encounter rate $\lambda_{\text{film}}$ requires empirical data from historical maintenance logs.

Aisle navigation introduces a second register entry: obstacle dynamics. Stopping-distance budgets are formulated to avoid stationary obstacles. A pedestrian who continues walking toward the mobile base throughout the braking maneuver consumes clearance distance that the stopping budget does not allocate (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion). As demonstrated in @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes, accounting for continuous human approach velocity caps the permissible base speed at the rack intersection far below normal transit velocities. The underlying safety premise assumes that pedestrians do not approach the rack corner during an emergency stop, leaving pedestrian presence in the occluded cross aisle as an unobserved state. Restricted service therefore requires physical barriers or facility access controls that prevent human cross-traffic during automated transit; painted floor warnings do not satisfy this condition. Facility operations owns this operational restriction. A proposed blind-corner presence sensor cannot be credited in the safety case until its detection field, latency, and reliability pass formal qualification using the zero-failure statistical criteria established earlier in this section.

The automated picking station contributes a third entry, governing manipulator interaction. This premise asserts that an object grasped by the end-effector—and subsequently handed to a human coworker via the `accept_item` interface (@sec-intervention-human-authority)—matches the precise object requested by the task planner. As revealed in @sec-intent-request-to-proposal, semantic grounding can fail silently: when a thin-walled red glass jar is positioned adjacent to a red ceramic mug on the takeaway conveyor, the grounding model confidently selects the jar, satisfying every geometric tolerance in the planner and permission layers. The missing observables are object identity and structural fragility, which neither wrist cameras nor visual foundation models can reliably verify prior to physical contact.

Mitigating this hazard requires a two-part operational restriction. First, facility operations restricts conveyor loading strictly to verified items from a declared SKU manifest that excludes fragile look-alikes. Second, the pick station admits grasp execution only when optical singulation confirms exactly one object in the pick zone; the presence of multiple objects aborts the automated intent and flags the item for manual picking. Singulation eliminates geometric ambiguity among permitted items but provides no independent confirmation of material composition; an off-manifest glass jar arriving in isolation is contained solely by upstream loading procedures. Setting a global grip-force threshold low enough to protect fragile items would require establishing crush limits for every inventory item—itself an unverified physical assumption. Facility operations and the application engineering team co-own the item catalog and singulation protocols. The closure test requires qualifying an automated identification mechanism at the workstation—such as an RFID scanner or an integrated scale-and-barcode reader—with a false-accept rate bounded at `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_pct_str` at `{python} OilFilm.confidence_pct_str` confidence across `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` failure-free trials with seeded look-alikes.

@Tbl-17-claims-register compares these three entries side by side, documenting the four required architectural components for each open premise.

\Needspace{31\baselineskip}

|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
