: **Residual-claims register for the aisle and the pick station**: Proposed responses to three open premises behind the mobile manipulator's aisle speed and its pick; operating credit requires the supporting evidence stipulated in the restricted-service branch. For each, the register names the missing physical observable, the hazard it permits, the operating restriction and its accountable owner, and the predeclared closure test that would retire the restriction. {#tbl-17-claims-register tbl-colwidths="[22,24,26,28]"}

The register also maintains the unresolved timing premise from @sec-placement. Measured capture-to-dispatch latency excludes downstream dispatch-to-admission processing. In @sec-placement, this duration is budgeted at `{python} OilFilm.delta_da_str` out of the total `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str` timing allowance at nominal aisle velocity, reserving `{python} OilFilm.reserve_da_str` of execution margin. This allocation represents an engineering budget rather than an empirical measurement, and steady-state inference benchmarks do not bound worst-case admission delays. The runtime systems team owns the loaded empirical qualification of both latency intervals against the lease duration and renewal requirements established in the execution contracts. Until physical measurements validate this timing allocation and confirm positive margin, nominal aisle speeds remain uncertified candidates. While the stipulated service regime assumes supporting timing evidence for its derated mode, this open item remains unclosed in the baseline system records.

Production release pipelines format each register entry according to a standardized data schema; detailed wire formats, data fields, and structural invariants are documented in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-residual-claims.

#### Maintaining the restrictions {#sec-frontier-operationalizing-claims}

Operational restrictions recorded in the register must couple directly to the runtime enforcement mechanisms and physical workflows that govern site execution. Cryptographically signed velocity envelopes constrain the onboard permission path, while mandated maintenance intervals bind facility operations. Deployment pipelines verify that both constraints exist in the authorized system configuration, whereas runtime monitors enforce only the physical properties accessible through onboard telemetry. Formatting an unobserved assumption into a machine-readable data schema does not transform it into a measured physical state.

Model retraining or software reconfiguration must inherit all unresolved restrictions whose empirical claims remain unproven. Deployment gates must validate signed operational limits and underlying evidentiary status prior to authorizing operational execution. Downgrading to a restricted mode requires its own validated safety case; an unresolved register entry does not grant automatic operational clearance. At runtime, low-level controllers enforce speed ceilings and actuator limits, while facility personnel maintain surface friction and conveyor feed protocols at qualified operational intervals.

When an unverified proposal is rejected, the system falls back to the state-dependent contingency maneuvers established in @sec-enforcement. Rejecting a newly proposed trajectory does not invalidate an executing trajectory chunk whose lease, state estimate, and safety envelope remain sound. However, the complete loss of active permission demands an immediate, physically feasible stopping response within the remaining stopping budget. Systems engineers must distinguish between controlled dynamic deceleration, holding brakes at zero velocity, actuator torque disablement, and complete power isolation: each produces vastly different transient dynamics, and no software registry can replace these physical distinctions with a generic emergency-stop primitive.

Novel sensing modalities can justify expanded operational envelopes only after formal empirical qualification. Where real-time detection remains infeasible, designers must rely on conservative trajectories, passive mechanical compliance, periodic proof-testing, or restricted operational design domains. Selecting among these mitigations requires evaluating what physical hazards can unfold before the system crosses its hard physical deadline.

### Failures without detectors {#sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors}

An automated floor-film detector can validate the surface friction premise only if its coverage, false-alarm rate, and detection latency satisfy route-specific kinematic constraints. These requirements represent application-specific engineering bounds rather than arbitrary model benchmarks. In the known-component stopping analysis, operating at candidate aisle velocity leaves `{python} OilFilm.spare_aisle_str` of physical margin, corresponding to an allowable delay of `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str`. Allocating `{python} OilFilm.delta_da_str` to dispatch-to-admission processing leaves `{python} OilFilm.reserve_da_str` of timing reserve. This margin represents an absolute upper bound on unallocated latency, not a certified budget for new perception pipelines. Furthermore, this timing allowance provides zero protection against a pedestrian who continues walking toward the vehicle throughout the stopping maneuver.

A forward-looking fluid detector faces an even more demanding kinematic deadline. The required detection range, minus the distance traversed during sensor integration and neural inference latency, must accommodate the full dry-floor stopping distance prior to the machine reaching the film's leading boundary:
$$d_{\text{detect}} \ge v\,t_{\text{detect}} + d_{\text{budget}}(v),$$ {#eq-frontier-film-detection-range}
where $d_{\text{budget}}(v)$ denotes the completed dry-floor stopping budget defined in @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget. Assuming an aggressive perception latency of `{python} OilFilm.t_detect_str` at nominal velocity `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str`, the sensor must detect surface contamination at least `{python} OilFilm.d_detect_min_str` in advance. This requirement consumes virtually the entire `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clearance distance to the rack end, because sensor processing consumes nearly all of the available `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str` timing allowance, leaving no margin for the `{python} OilFilm.delta_da_str` dispatch-to-admission interval. If classification occurs only after the drive wheels enter the fluid, the stopping distance expands to `{python} OilFilm.stop_oil_str`, vastly exceeding the `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` physical clearance. Sensory classifications received after the wheels cross onto the contaminant can serve forensic incident analysis, but they arrive too late to avert a collision.

#### Observational indistinguishability and the action deadline {#sec-frontier-observational-indistinguishability-sub}

The fundamental limit of runtime safety filtering stems from observational indistinguishability. Consider two physical world states, $S_A$ and $S_B$. In state $S_A$, a commanded actuator trajectory $u(t)$ executes safely. In state $S_B$, that identical control input $u(t)$ triggers catastrophic structural damage or human injury, requiring the permission system to intervene with an emergency stop. The physical constraint governing this response is distance rather than elapsed time. Because deceleration alters the spatial trajectory, the point of harm is a physical coordinate. Let $d_{\text{rem}}$ represent the remaining distance to that boundary when the discriminating observation arrives. An emergency stop completes safely short of the hazard only if:
$$d_{\text{rem}} \ge v\,(t_{\text{enforce}} + t_{\text{actuation}}) + d_{\text{brake}}(v),$$ {#eq-frontier-action-deadline}
matching the physical stopping formulation applied throughout this book since @sec-body, where $d_{\text{brake}}(v)$ is the braking distance of the chosen stopping maneuver. Dividing this spatial constraint by the approach velocity yields an equivalent observation deadline: $t_{\text{deadline}} = t_{\text{harm}} - t_{\text{enforce}} - t_{\text{actuation}} - d_{\text{brake}}(v)/v$, where $t_{\text{harm}}$ denotes the moment the unbraked trajectory would reach the point of impact. A common engineering error subtracts the full stopping duration $t_{\text{brake}}$ rather than the velocity-normalized distance $d_{\text{brake}}/v$, implicitly assuming the vehicle maintains constant velocity until coming to an instantaneous halt. For the jerk-limited profile from `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str`, braking lasts `{python} OilFilm.t_brake_aisle_str` but traverses a distance equivalent to only `{python} OilFilm.t_brake_equiv_str` of constant-velocity travel. Formulating the deadline purely in time over-reserves `{python} OilFilm.t_overreserve_str`, or `{python} OilFilm.d_overreserve_str` of spatial clearance—an error that exceeds the entire `{python} OilFilm.spare_aisle_str` margin. Manipulator contact introduces an analogous coupled dynamic: once an end-effector contacts a rigid surface, contact force rather than spatial position dictates the observation deadline (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_stop_time_overreserve_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three horizontal bars in milliseconds. The top bar, labeled stop lasts, totals 931.2 milliseconds: a slate part of 465.6 milliseconds and a red extension labeled plus 465.6 milliseconds over. The middle bar, labeled distance divided by v, is 465.6 milliseconds and ends at a dotted line where the red extension begins. The bottom bar, labeled whole spare, is a short gray bar of 100.8 milliseconds."}

*Charging the full stop time over-reserves several times the entire spare.*
:::

If the observation telemetry $y(t)$ generated under state $S_A$ is identical to that under $S_B$ up to $t_{\text{deadline}}$ for every admissible control input, no software algorithm operating on those observations can discriminate the safe state from the hazardous state in time to prevent harm. This condition defines observational indistinguishability:

::: {#dfn-frontier-observational-indistinguishability .callout-definition title="Observational indistinguishability"}

***Observational indistinguishability***\index{Observational indistinguishability!definition} is the condition in which two physical states that require different responses produce the same observation history, under every input the machine may admissibly apply, until the deadline by which a state-specific response must begin.

1.  **Significance**: It turns an observation limit into a stopping-budget violation. The deadline is set by @eq-frontier-action-deadline, so if the film and the dry floor look identical until the remaining distance falls below $v\,(t_{\text{enforce}} + t_{\text{actuation}}) + d_{\text{brake}}(v)$, no response chosen on that evidence can keep $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$ for the hazardous state.
2.  **Distinction**: Noise and weak detectors obscure information that more data or a better model can recover; indistinguishability means the information is absent from the channel. Unlike classical unobservability, which asks whether a state can ever be reconstructed, it is tied to a deadline and to the inputs the machine may apply.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that a more capable classifier on the same channel will eventually separate the states. Identical histories give every classifier identical inputs, so only a new channel, a designed probe, or a response valid in both states changes the outcome.

:::

The qualification regarding *every admissible input* is essential. State distinguishability depends directly on system excitation, as formalized in nonlinear observability theory [@hermann1977nonlinear]. In specific settings, an engineer can synthesize an active control perturbation that forces the states to diverge observationally before the critical deadline. This technique is known as **active probing**\index{Active probing!definition}: the deliberate injection of a bounded excitation designed to expose hidden state differences within the observation channel prior to the action deadline. Active probing builds upon the principles of auxiliary signal design[^fn-auxiliary-signal-design] developed for fault detection [@campbell2004auxiliary]. For example, applying a controlled pre-contact tug on a door latch below its yield ceiling, or commanding a momentary micro-torque pulse on a known floor patch, transforms an unobserved physical property into measurable telemetry. The operational cost of active probing is latency and dynamic disturbance, both of which must respect system safety bounds. Where no admissible probing action can safely separate the states within the timing budget, designers must fall back on conservative worst-case trajectories or passive physical containment.

[^fn-auxiliary-signal-design]: **Auxiliary Signal Design**\index{Auxiliary signal design!active fault detection}: The multimodel method computes a small test input that guarantees the normal model and each declared failure model produce different outputs within a fixed test horizon, despite bounded disturbances [@campbell2004auxiliary]. A probe can therefore rule out only the failures someone wrote down as models, which is why the hidden premise must first be named in the register. The input bound and the horizon map onto this chapter's budgets, since the probe must fit the force envelope and the separation must arrive before $t_{\text{deadline}}$.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The observation contract of @sec-perception-observation-contract bounds the age and error of what a channel reports; it cannot certify a state the channel never carries.
:::

#### Responses when the state remains hidden {#sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment}

When physical states remain observationally indistinguishable prior to an action deadline, software algorithms cannot execute state-specific branching logic. Under these conditions, exactly four engineering alternatives remain: injecting an admissible active probe to reveal the state before the deadline, executing a conservative maneuver that remains safe across both candidate states, enforcing passive mechanical compliance or physical proof-testing to bound interaction forces, or withholding operational authority entirely.

Sensor degradation exhibits identical observability barriers across extended operating horizons. Strain-gauge force-torque sensors at the robot wrist drift over time as mechanical stress relaxation and ambient thermal cycles alter bridge resistance. A sensor experiencing negative baseline drift produces a telemetry profile indistinguishable from an interaction that genuinely applies lower contact force. Because a single transducer reports only a scalar wrench component, no software algorithm processing that data stream can differentiate between genuine physical compliance and calibration drift. Without an external reference—such as a periodic unloaded tare or physical proof-test fixture—internal telemetry cannot detect sensor drift at runtime.

A structurally degraded door latch presents the same observability barrier on a millisecond timescale. Prior to mechanical failure, joint torque sensors record identical forces against a weakened latch as against a sound latch: both supply the identical reaction force, and the torque channel contains zero information regarding remaining yield margin. Mechanical yield is plastic and irreversible; no software command issued after yield occurs can undo the damage. Consequently, running faster classification models on joint torque signals provides zero protection. Defensible safety strategies must inject information that the sensing channel lacks. Periodic proof tests[^fn-proof-test-interval] verify latch yield strength at scheduled intervals. However, a proof-testing strategy remains valid only if maintenance records confirm that material fatigue, wear, and corrosion cannot degrade the latch's yield threshold below the robot's contact ceiling between consecutive test intervals.

[^fn-proof-test-interval]: **Proof Test**\index{Proof test!interval}: Functional safety defines a proof test as a periodic test that reveals dangerous failures no online diagnostic can detect, so that the function can be restored to its as-new condition [@iec61508]. A hidden failure that arrives at a constant rate $\lambda$ is present, on average over a test interval $T$, for a fraction of about $\lambda T/2$ of the time when $\lambda T$ is small. The interval is therefore itself a safety parameter, because it bounds how long a weakened latch can go unseen.

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-latch-compliance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ A SERIES COMPLIANT ELEMENT AT THE DOOR LATCH
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment,
# │          @eq-frontier-passive-compliance.
# │ Goal:    Size the stiffness and stroke of a series spring that lets the
# │          arm meet the latch at the faster approach speed without passing
# │          the declared force floor, using the registry's latch values.
# │ Show:    rigid-plate result at both approach speeds; the stiffness bound;
# │          the element stiffness, stroke, and the peak if torque is removed.
# │ How:     after the tripwire, the arm travels v t_resp + v^2/(2 a_arm)
# │          (calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile, the Ch10 model); the force
# │          condition F_trip + k_eq * stroke <= F_floor bounds the series
# │          stiffness k_eq; springs in series give the element stiffness; a
# │          coasting mass stores m v^2/2 on top of the tripwire energy.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics import calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchCompliance:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Registry and chosen design inputs) ──────────────────────────
    k_plate = AISLE.k_latch  # category: illustrative (strike-plate contact stiffness)
    v_guarded = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: illustrative (guarded approach, the declared ODD)
    v_fast = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (faster approach the policy proposes)
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: chosen (contact tripwire)
    t_resp = AISLE.t_contact_response  # category: illustrative (tripwire to brake onset)
    f_floor = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative (declared force floor, a judgment, not a measured strength)
    m_eff = RM.arm_effective_contact_mass  # category: derived (robot-side effective mass at the TCP)
    f_pre = 0.0 * ureg.newton  # category: chosen (series spring without preload)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    rigid_guarded = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(scenario=AISLE)
    rigid_fast = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(approach_velocity=v_fast, scenario=AISLE)
    a_arm = rigid_guarded["a_arm_needed"].to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)  # hold the arm to the guarded approach's stop
    a_arm_fast_rigid = rigid_fast["a_arm_needed"].to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)

    stroke_fast = (v_fast * t_resp + v_fast**2 / (2 * a_arm)).to(ureg.millimeter)  # driven stroke after the tripwire
    k_eq_max = ((f_floor - f_trip) / stroke_fast).to(ureg.newton / ureg.meter)
    k_spring_max = (1 / (1 / k_eq_max - 1 / k_plate)).to(ureg.newton / ureg.meter)
    stroke_needed = ((f_floor - f_pre) / k_spring_max).to(ureg.millimeter)  # element deflection at the floor force

    def coast_peak(k, v, m, f0):
        # Peak force if drive torque is removed at the tripwire: f0^2/(2k) + m v^2/2 = F^2/(2k)
        return (f0**2 + k * m * v**2) ** 0.5

    f_coast_rigid_guarded = coast_peak(k_plate, v_guarded, m_eff, f_trip).to(ureg.newton)
    f_coast_rigid_fast = coast_peak(k_plate, v_fast, m_eff, f_trip).to(ureg.newton)
    f_coast_compliant_fast = coast_peak(k_eq_max, v_fast, m_eff, f_trip).to(ureg.newton)
    check_profile = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(approach_velocity=v_fast, latch_stiffness=k_eq_max, scenario=AISLE)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(a_arm.magnitude - 2.9508) < 5e-4, f"Guarded-approach arm stop should be 2.95 m/s^2, got {a_arm}.")
    check(abs(a_arm_fast_rigid.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-6, f"Rigid plate at the fast approach needs 400 m/s^2, got {a_arm_fast_rigid}.")
    check(abs(stroke_fast.magnitude - 1.8944) < 5e-4, f"Driven stroke at the fast approach should be 1.89 mm, got {stroke_fast}.")
    check(abs(k_eq_max.magnitude - 44868.0) < 5.0, f"Series stiffness bound should be 44.9 kN/m, got {k_eq_max}.")
    check(abs(k_spring_max.magnitude - 50537.0) < 5.0, f"Element stiffness should be 50.5 kN/m, got {k_spring_max}.")
    check(abs(stroke_needed.magnitude - 1.979) < 5e-3, f"Element stroke should be 1.98 mm, got {stroke_needed}.")
    check(k_eq_max < k_plate, "The fast approach needs a softer load path than the rigid plate.")
    check(abs(check_profile["a_arm_needed"].magnitude - a_arm.magnitude) < 1e-6, "With k_eq at the bound, the Ch10 model needs the same arm stop.")
    check(f_coast_rigid_guarded < f_floor, "At the guarded approach the rigid plate stays under the floor even if torque is removed.")
    check(f_coast_rigid_fast > 2 * f_floor, "At the fast approach the rigid plate more than doubles the floor.")
    check(f_coast_compliant_fast < f_floor, "With the element, removing torque at the tripwire stays under the floor.")
    # margin_latch_coasting_peak_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 67, 220, 75 and 100 N, 0.03 and 0.1 m/s
    check(abs(f_coast_rigid_guarded.magnitude - 67.4) < 0.05, f"Rigid guarded coasting peak should be 67.4 N, got {f_coast_rigid_guarded}.")
    check(abs(f_coast_rigid_fast.magnitude - 219.6) < 0.05, f"Rigid fast coasting peak should be 219.6 N, got {f_coast_rigid_fast}.")
    check(abs(f_coast_compliant_fast.magnitude - 74.9) < 0.05, f"Compliant fast coasting peak should be 74.9 N, got {f_coast_compliant_fast}.")
    check(abs(f_floor.magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9, f"Declared force floor should be 100 N, got {f_floor}.")
    check(
        abs(v_guarded.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9 and abs(v_fast.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 0.1) < 1e-9,
        "Approach speeds should be 0.03 and 0.1 m/s.",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    k_plate_str = fmt_sci_qty(k_plate, ureg.newton / ureg.meter, precision=1)
    v_guarded_str = fmt_velocity(v_guarded, precision=2)
    v_fast_str = fmt_velocity(v_fast, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
    t_resp_str = fmt_latency(t_resp, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    f_floor_str = fmt_force(f_floor, precision=0)
    m_eff_str = fmt_mass(m_eff, unit=ureg.kg, precision=0)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm, precision=2)
    a_arm_fast_rigid_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm_fast_rigid, precision=0)
    stroke_fast_str = fmt_length(stroke_fast, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    k_eq_max_str = fmt_qty(k_eq_max.to(ureg.kilonewton / ureg.meter), unit=ureg.kilonewton / ureg.meter, precision=1)
    k_spring_max_str = fmt_qty(k_spring_max.to(ureg.kilonewton / ureg.meter), unit=ureg.kilonewton / ureg.meter, precision=1)
    stroke_needed_str = fmt_length(stroke_needed, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    f_coast_rigid_guarded_str = fmt_force(f_coast_rigid_guarded, precision=1)
    f_coast_rigid_fast_str = fmt_force(f_coast_rigid_fast, precision=1)
    f_coast_compliant_fast_str = fmt_force(f_coast_compliant_fast, precision=1)
```

Integrating a passive compliant element into the mechanical structure can physically limit transmitted interaction forces across a qualified deflection stroke—the foundational principle underlying series elastic actuators [@pratt1995series] and mechanical torque limiters. Two physical conditions govern compliant load paths, both determined by the stroke the arm *actively drives* following contact detection rather than the total uncompressed spring length. When a contact tripwire $F_{\text{trip}}$ triggers, the manipulator continues moving during its controller response latency $t_{\text{resp}}$ before decelerating at rate $a_{\text{arm}}$, driving the mechanism through a post-contact displacement of $\Delta x_{\text{driven}} = v\,t_{\text{resp}} + v^2/(2a_{\text{arm}})$. To prevent the interaction force from exceeding the declared structural threshold $F_{\text{floor}}$, the equivalent stiffness $k_{\text{eq}}$ of the combined series load path (compliant element and strike plate) must satisfy @eq-frontier-passive-compliance:
$$F_{\text{trip}} + k_{\text{eq}}\,\Delta x_{\text{driven}} \le F_{\text{floor}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k_{\text{eq}} \le \frac{F_{\text{floor}}-F_{\text{trip}}}{v\,t_{\text{resp}} + v^2/(2a_{\text{arm}})}.$$ {#eq-frontier-passive-compliance}
In addition, the compliant element's allowable stroke must exceed its deflection under the peak allowable force, $(F_{\text{floor}}-F_{\text{preload}})/k_{\text{spring}}$, ensuring the mechanism never bottoms out into a rigid mechanical stop. The threshold $F_{\text{floor}}$ does not represent the latch's actual physical yield strength, which remains unobserved between proof tests; rather, it represents the lower bound on yield strength established through accountable engineering judgment and documented in the system register.

The warehouse door latch demonstrates the concrete protection provided by passive compliance. During a guarded approach at `{python} LatchCompliance.v_guarded_str`, interacting with a rigid strike plate of stiffness `{python} LatchCompliance.k_plate_str` satisfies @eq-frontier-passive-compliance with a required arm deceleration of `{python} LatchCompliance.a_arm_str`, consistent with the kinematic budget established in @sec-intent-handoff. However, at an elevated approach velocity of `{python} LatchCompliance.v_fast_str`, the same rigid contact would require an impossible arm deceleration of `{python} LatchCompliance.a_arm_fast_rigid_str`, compelling the safety layer to reject the trajectory. By constraining arm deceleration to the guarded stopping bound, the manipulator drives through a displacement of `{python} LatchCompliance.stroke_fast_str` after triggering the `{python} LatchCompliance.f_trip_str` tripwire, capping the allowable series stiffness at `{python} LatchCompliance.k_eq_max_str`. Because series compliance combines inversely ($1/k_{\text{eq}} = 1/k_{\text{spring}} + 1/k_{\text{plate}}$), coupling the compliant element with the strike plate demands a spring stiffness no greater than `{python} LatchCompliance.k_spring_max_str` and an available stroke of at least `{python} LatchCompliance.stroke_needed_str` to withstand the `{python} LatchCompliance.f_floor_str` design force.

This quasi-static formulation assumes the actuator drive actively applies braking torque throughout the post-tripwire stroke. If the safety response instead cuts motor torque completely, the arm's effective inertia `{python} LatchCompliance.m_eff_str` coasts dynamically into the compliant element, where peak force is governed by conservation of energy. A spring compressed to force $F$ stores potential energy $F^2/(2k_{\text{eq}})$; at tripwire detection, the spring already contains $F_{\text{trip}}^2/(2k_{\text{eq}})$, and the coasting mass adds its full kinetic energy $m_{\text{eff}}v^2/2$. The resulting peak impact force is $\sqrt{F_{\text{trip}}^2 + k_{\text{eq}}\,m_{\text{eff}}\,v^2}$—the dynamic impact regime that dominates high-speed robotic collisions [@haddadin2009requirements]. With the compliant element installed, this coasting peak evaluates to `{python} LatchCompliance.f_coast_compliant_fast_str`. In contrast, striking the rigid plate without compliance yields peak forces of `{python} LatchCompliance.f_coast_rigid_fast_str` at high approach velocity and `{python} LatchCompliance.f_coast_rigid_guarded_str` under guarded approach. The compliant element guarantees that transmitted forces remain below the latch's declared design strength regardless of software state. However, passive compliance does not verify structural latch integrity: system qualification must empirically validate dynamic damping, material fatigue, and structural load paths rather than spring stiffness alone.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_latch_coasting_peak_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three amber bars of peak latch force against a red dashed line labeled 100 newton floor, with the region beyond it shaded. A rigid plate at 0.03 m/s reaches 67 newtons, under the line. A rigid plate at 0.1 m/s reaches 220 newtons, far past it. A series spring at 0.1 m/s reaches 75 newtons, under the line."}

*A series spring keeps the coasting peak under the declared `{python} LatchCompliance.f_floor_str` floor.*
:::

The door latch, the surface oil film, and the packaging tab share an identical systems challenge. When an essential safety premise cannot be evaluated prior to an execution deadline, systems engineers must select among active probing, conservative universal control actions, passive mechanical boundaries, periodic physical proof-testing, or restricted operational design domains. The selection is governed by the specific operational claim each strategy can substantiate and the physical evidence required to maintain it. Furthermore, every architectural mitigation must define the exact empirical criteria required to retire it, delineating the physical and epistemic boundaries of the machine.

::: {#chk-frontier-hidden-premises .callout-checkpoint title="Premises no sensor reports"}

The warehouse machine's hardest limits are premises its own telemetry cannot check, and each one needs an entry, a restriction, and a response chosen before the deadline.

- [ ] **Friction estimate**: A friction survey measures an aisle at $\mu$ = `{python} OilFilm.mu_check_str`. Given the `{python} OilFilm.a_brake_str` braking bound, can you compute the credible deceleration from @eq-frontier-credible-deceleration and say whether the brake or the floor binds?
- [ ] **Register entry**: For the weakened door latch, can you state the four components of its register entry, the missing observable, the restriction, the owner, and the closure test?
- [ ] **Shield credit**: Why does @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard give no credit against the oil film, and which term would the film enter?
- [ ] **Hidden-state responses**: When two states stay indistinguishable until the deadline, which responses remain, and which of them does the series spring at the latch represent?

:::
## Choosing the Next Capability {#sec-frontier-assumptions-change}

In a deployed packaging cell, restricted transit speeds and human-supervised sign-offs drive fundamentally different research investments. Accelerating proposal generation improves throughput within the current safety envelope, whereas qualifying a new contact or engagement sensor can retire the need for human sign-off entirely. Each advance demands two deliverables: a predeclared task metric and an empirical test of the operational premise it modifies. Optimizing execution inside an existing envelope and producing the evidence required to expand that envelope represent related but distinct engineering programs.

### What a restriction costs {#sec-frontier-deployment-economics}

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-restriction-cost
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PRICE OF A RESTRICTION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-frontier-deployment-economics.
# │ Goal:    Price the oil-film entry's restricted mode in the one unit that
# │          holds on every site, time per aisle leg, and set it beside the
# │          size of the campaigns that would retire it.
# │ Show:    the speed cut, cruise time per leg at both speeds, the added time,
# │          and the closure and coverage campaign sizes from the cells above.
# │ How:     cruise time = leg length / speed (acceleration and stops omitted,
# │          so the figure is a lower bound on the added time).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class RestrictionCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_nominal = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen (normal-mode aisle speed)
    v_restricted = OilFilm.v_restricted  # category: chosen (restricted mode on inspected floors)
    leg = AISLE.aisle_length  # category: illustrative (aisle length)
    totes_reported = 100_000  # category: measured, vendor-reported (Agility Robotics, 20 Nov 2025: Digit at GXO Flowery Branch)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    speed_cut = (1 - v_restricted / v_nominal).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    t_leg_nominal = (leg / v_nominal).to(ureg.second)
    t_leg_restricted = (leg / v_restricted).to(ureg.second)
    t_leg_added = (t_leg_restricted - t_leg_nominal).to(ureg.second)
    time_increase = (t_leg_added / t_leg_nominal).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(speed_cut - 0.2308) < 5e-4, f"Speed cut should be 23.1 percent, got {speed_cut}.")
    check(abs(t_leg_nominal.magnitude - 23.077) < 5e-3, f"Nominal leg should take 23.1 s, got {t_leg_nominal}.")
    check(abs(t_leg_restricted.magnitude - 30.0) < 1e-9, f"Restricted leg should take 30.0 s, got {t_leg_restricted}.")
    check(abs(time_increase - 0.30) < 1e-9, f"Leg time should rise 30 percent, got {time_increase}.")
    check(time_increase > speed_cut, "A speed cut lengthens the leg by more than its own percentage.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_nominal_str = fmt_velocity(v_nominal, precision=1)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, precision=0)
    leg_str = fmt_length(leg, unit=ureg.meter, precision=0)
    speed_cut_str = fmt_percent(speed_cut, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_leg_nominal_str = fmt_latency(t_leg_nominal, unit=ureg.second, precision=1)
    t_leg_restricted_str = fmt_latency(t_leg_restricted, unit=ureg.second, precision=0)
    time_increase_str = fmt_percent(time_increase, precision=0, style="prose")
    totes_reported_str = fmt_int(totes_reported, commas=True)
```

Every entry in the residual-claims register purchases physical protection at the expense of operational throughput. In our warehouse baseline, the oil-film restriction lowers cruising speed along the aisle from `{python} RestrictionCost.v_nominal_str` to `{python} RestrictionCost.v_restricted_str`, imposing a `{python} RestrictionCost.speed_cut_str` speed penalty. At steady cruise, this derating stretches transit time across each `{python} RestrictionCost.leg_str` aisle segment from `{python} RestrictionCost.t_leg_nominal_str` to `{python} RestrictionCost.t_leg_restricted_str`. That single constraint adds `{python} RestrictionCost.time_increase_str` more transit time per leg before accounting for acceleration profiles and docking maneuvers. Because transit time scales nonlinearly as $1/v$, the percentage increase in cycle time substantially outstrips the percentage reduction in speed.

An operational restriction remains in force until its closure test passes. That test carries a tangible empirical cost: either the `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` seeded-film physical trials specified in the register, or the `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_coverage_str` seeded hazardous proposals required to establish safety shield coverage. The claims register therefore confronts systems engineers with an economic optimization problem alongside the technical one. Mounting a formal closure campaign makes financial sense only when the cumulative throughput lost to the restriction exceeds the combined cost of the test campaign and the sensing instrument it qualifies. Conversely, an operational restriction remains the superior choice when its underlying premise is cheap to maintain administratively, such as enforcing standard floor-cleaning protocols along a few pallet-jack routes. Evaluating this trade-off requires site-specific parameters: the economic value of a completed task, the machine's active duty hours on restricted routes, and the marginal expense of executing controlled test trials. In the absence of proprietary site economics, time provides the universal benchmark that transfers directly across facilities.

The same operational accounting governs fleet deployments. When commercial logistics facilities contract bipedal humanoids under robots-as-a-service agreements [@gxo2024agility], commercial performance is measured strictly by volume moved—reaching `{python} RestrictionCost.totes_reported_str` totes at an initial customer facility by late 2025 [@agility2025totes]. In these operational environments, every physical intervention, speed restriction, and withheld autonomy mode directly reduces billing throughput. The gating criteria established during release validation (@sec-release) translate directly into ongoing operating expenses.
Intervention rates incur a double cost. Frequent human takeovers consume costly labor hours and tether fleet operations to local technician availability. Conversely, rare interventions introduce the classic ironies of automation: an operator who seldom intervenes struggles to maintain the situational awareness and manual dexterity needed when an emergency takeover occurs [@bainbridge1983ironies]. A defensible business case therefore reports proposer autonomy, whole-machine task success, and protective responses separately, as the first fallacy below insists, because each carries a different price.

### Who bears the costs that safety does not count {#sec-frontier-workforce-accountability}

The accounting above prices an operational restriction purely in machine cycle time. In practice, automated deployments also shift burdens onto human workers—costs that traditional product-safety certifications never measure. When an autonomous mobile manipulator operates in a warehouse, the labor required to move a tote never truly vanishes. Instead, physical tasks shift to the human specialists who assume manual teleoperation whenever a motion planner stalls (@sec-intervention), technicians who physically sweep and inspect restricted transit corridors, and facility crews who maintain the environmental assumptions codified in the claims register. The intervention frequency logged during release testing defines the operational profile of human labor: technician dispatch frequency, required response latencies, and physical staging locations across the facility floor. Across United States local labor markets, greater exposure to fixed industrial robotics between 1990 and 2007 depressed both employment rates and wages [@acemoglu2020robots]. Whether mobile collaborative manipulators in logistics will follow that historical pattern has not yet been measured at scale. The operational audit trails designed in this book provide the precise empirical data required for such investigations, capturing tasks completed, manual takeovers, and technician hours dedicated to each route.

System accountability extends beyond physical product safety into operational governance. While conformity assessment under the European Union Machinery Regulation certifies that an autonomous machine can operate safely alongside human workers, regulatory compliance alone does not govern how telemetry records are used downstream. An embodied system's authority logs and black-box flight recorders capture the identity of every human operator initiating a manual takeover. If an enterprise repurposes these telemetry streams to score employee performance, the infrastructure crosses a significant legal threshold. Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, Annex III explicitly classifies AI systems intended to monitor and evaluate employee performance as high-risk systems, while Article 26 mandates that employers formally notify employee representatives and affected workers prior to workplace deployment [@eu2024aiact]. Our system architecture addresses this risk by treating governance metadata as an enforceable invariant. Every generated record explicitly specifies its declared operational purpose, data owner, and authorized access control policies. Predeployment release validation treats these contractual boundaries as standing conditions (@sec-release-recorded-people), ensuring that audit logs recorded for safety incident reconstruction cannot be silently repurposed for employee evaluation. By enforcing these architectural boundaries, an embodied platform assigns clear operational accountability for its workforce impact, mirroring how it tracks every physical residual claim.

### Proposal is not permission, in law {#sec-frontier-thesis-in-law}

In this book, the third architectural law—that a learned proposal is not permission—becomes a statutory mandate for machinery placed on the European Union market. The Machinery Regulation, whose enforcement dates and jurisdictional scope are detailed in @sec-release-standards-map, explicitly identifies safety components "with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine learning approaches ensuring safety functions," and the machinery embedding them, as high-risk categories whose conformity requires assessment by a notified body (Annex I, Part A) [@eu2023machinery]. Its essential health and safety requirements establish the operational boundary: the limits of safety functions must be formally documented in the manufacturer's risk assessment, and no rule or parameter generated by the machine, even during an active learning phase, may modify those limits whenever the change could induce a hazardous condition (Annex III, Section 1.2.1).

Mapped directly to our system architecture, European Union statutory requirements formalize the proposal boundary. The pivotal regulatory distinction centers on whether a learned component executes or ensures a certified safety function. When a learned neural proposer generates candidate actions that reach motor drives only through an independent permission pipeline with fixed, cryptographically signed limits, the learned model does not ensure a safety function. Instead, safety enforcement rests exclusively on certified, deterministic components: the safety-rated drive functions and laser scanners detailed in @tbl-12-certified-functions, accompanied by a dedicated safety microcontroller executing a hardware lease watchdog that asserts Safe Torque Off (STO) or Safe Stop 1 (SS1) on the drives whenever software permission lapses. Upstream admission filters—such as control barrier function projections, kinodynamic feasibility checks, and message freshness tests—shape proposal generation within nominal limits set by formal risk assessments rather than learned heuristics.
By contrast, if an embodied system relies on a learned neural component to ensure a protective function—such as a deep vision detector acting as the primary perimeter guard, or an end-to-end policy streaming torque commands to motor drives without independent admission filtering—the learned module falls under Annex I, Part A and requires third-party assessment. System architecture directly determines regulatory certification pathways, although final determinations remain subject to the manufacturer's risk assessment and notified body review. Here, the residual-claims register serves as the auditable artifact demanded by Section 1.2.1, formally documenting envelope boundaries, supporting verification evidence, and conditions prohibiting unverified online weight updates. How notified bodies will ultimately audit and certify high-dimensional learned policies whose closed-loop behaviors depend entirely on training distributions remains an open question as of 2026, as examined in @sec-frontier-four-open-challenges.

### Match the experiment to the missing evidence {#sec-frontier-four-gap-classes}

When an embodied platform encounters verification roadblocks, systems engineers must match the diagnostic experiment to the nature of the missing evidence:

- *Unmeasured observables* demand dedicated sensing modalities capable of distinguishing relevant physical states before dynamic control authority becomes ineffective.
- *Evaluation deficits* demand randomized field trials or statistical estimators that faithfully represent the operational population while accounting for sample dependence and rare tail risks.
- *Theoretical deficits* demand bounded analytical arguments whose governing physical assumptions can be mathematically or experimentally proven for the specific hardware plant.
- *Scope mismatches* demand structural modifications to the system architecture or a deliberate contraction of operational design domains.
Diagnosing the precise failure mode directs the next experiment, steering engineers away from the reflex of attempting to solve every residual claim with another neural detector.

Applying this taxonomy to our claims register separates unresolved engineering premises into actionable initiatives. Undetected surface oil slicks, occluded pedestrians, ambiguous object classifications, and misaligned packaging tabs are unmeasured observables; each demands either a qualified sensing channel with validated miss rates or an operational constraint that circumvents the hazard. Loaded dispatch-to-admission timing bounds and the empirical coverage metric $c_h$ for architectural safety shields represent evaluation deficits, resolved through randomized stress trials sampled across operational boundary states. Gaps between formal plant dynamics models and physical hardware constitute theoretical deficits (@sec-verification-formal-limits), requiring robust control bounds. Finally, attempting autonomous shipping sign-offs with an uncalibrated optical camera is a scope mismatch, corrected only by introducing downstream automated checkweighers or narrowing the autonomous operational domain.

Statistical extreme value theory (@sec-appendix-ml-evt) provides powerful tools for quantifying rare tail exceedances, provided that underlying asymptotic and independence assumptions hold. However, fitting a parametric distribution to empirical data cannot validate unmodeled contact physics or detect unobserved friction regimes. Similarly, Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis (@sec-appendix-control-hj-reachability) yields formal invariant sets only relative to an explicitly declared plant and bounded disturbance model. Shifting an unverified friction assumption from field testing into a rigid-body simulator or an analytical certificate merely relocates the epistemic debt without discharging the underlying engineering obligation.

### Research that changes an engineering result {#sec-frontier-four-open-challenges}

In physical AI, the open research problems that warrant industry and academic investment are those whose resolution directly alters a release gate verdict. As of 2026, six central challenges define the frontier of embodied machine learning. Each stresses one of the core architectural laws, maps directly to the gap taxonomy established earlier, and exhibits a measurable trajectory of empirical progress. @Tbl-17-frontier-agenda summarizes these challenges alongside contemporary benchmarks; the following discussions articulate the enduring systems principles underlying each.

Generalist and cross-embodiment policies fundamentally alter how systems engineers evaluate proposer boundaries. A single pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) foundation model can now control diverse kinematics. For example, flow-matching architectures have been trained across single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile manipulation platforms from a unified model [@black2024pi0], leveraging heterogeneous embodiment datasets (@sec-data-cross-embodiment). Modern pipelines continuously fine-tune from production deployments via reinforcement learning with human interventions [@physicalintelligence2025recap] or remap learned trajectories across distinct kinematic morphologies [@geminirobotics2025gemini15].
However, empirical safety evidence compiled on a dual-arm cobot cannot be assumed to hold when that same policy executes on a mobile manipulator. Furthermore, policies that continually adapt in production invalidate static release evidence gathered during predeployment audits (@sec-release-deployment-lifecycle). The enduring challenge is establishing formal transfer guarantees across both physical embodiments and continuous model updates. Concrete progress requires rigorous transfer arguments with explicit kinematic and dynamic equivalence conditions, verifiable by predicting a new morphology's closed-loop failure distributions prior to physical deployment. Crucially, this cross-embodiment paradigm reinforces the necessity of an independent permission pipeline: physical protection limits are calibrated to each specific mechanical chassis and remain invariant regardless of how frequently upstream generalist weights are updated.

Data scaling represents the empirical frontier of our second law (governing endogenous data distributions). Large-scale empirical studies encompassing more than 40,000 real-robot teleoperated demonstrations indicate that out-of-distribution generalization across novel environments and visual scenes follows an approximate power law governed by environmental diversity, whereas collecting redundant demonstrations within identical scenes exhibits sharp diminishing returns [@lin2025datascaling]. In physical systems, structural diversity rather than raw sample count dictates data utility (@sec-data-scaling-frontier).
The open challenge is determining whether these empirical scaling laws generalize to contact-rich manipulation, long-horizon multi-step planning, and safety-critical edge states. In embodied settings, an agent's closed-loop control actions actively determine its subsequent perceptual distributions, concentrating risk in rare, unmodeled corner cases. Meaningful progress requires publishing verified scaling curves that measure tail-risk closed-loop failure rates within declared operational design domains (ODDs), replacing benchmark evaluations that measure only average-case task completion rates.

Generative world models offer a promising strategy to bypass the physical exposure wall. Latent dynamics formulations and high-fidelity video generation models increasingly act as general-purpose physics simulators [@nvidia2025cosmos; @assran2025vjepa2]. Researchers have begun deploying these generative models directly as policy evaluators, demonstrating strong correlation with real-robot task execution on benchmark tasks [@jeon2026roboworld]. Synthetic rollouts execute at massive parallel scale for a fraction of the cost of physical hardware hours.
Nevertheless, fundamental epistemic limits constrain synthetic evaluation. A learned world model cannot supply physical state variables missing from its training inputs, nor can it faithfully extrapolate friction discontinuities or structural compliance omitted from its training distribution. The critical research question is establishing when synthetic evaluation in a learned world model constitutes valid evidentiary support for real-world release claims. Genuine progress requires formalizing proxy-transfer bounds (@sec-evaluation-proxy-transfer-law) validated against the empirical tail of real-world physical failures rather than aggregate nominal success, accompanied by end-to-end dataset and architecture provenance tracking (@sec-training-simulator-component).

Dynamically stable machines—such as bipedal humanoids and high-speed quadrupeds—represent the most stringent test of our first law (the physical irreversibility of actuation). As highlighted in Perspectives \ref{capstone-nervous-humanoid-crucible}, \ref{capstone-evaluation-humanoid-crucible}, \ref{capstone-placement-humanoid-crucible}, and \ref{capstone-release-humanoid-crucible}, the entire architectural chain of proposal, permission, and admission applies directly to balancing robots, with one catastrophic exception: fallback safe states.
On a wheeled platform or a stationary manipulator, the canonical safe fallback is to de-energize the actuators and apply mechanical brakes. On a balancing biped in mid-stride, cutting motor power induces an unrecoverable ballistic fall, transforming the safety mechanism into the primary hazard. Instead of bringing the system to an immediate stop, a balancing machine must execute dynamic recovery maneuvers: taking a stabilizing step, initiating a controlled crouch, or executing an active powered descent to a mechanically supported resting posture. Traditional functional safety standards, however, were architected around fail-passive de-energization, creating what safety researchers term the *fail-passive gap*[^fn-fail-passive-operational] [@ding2026failpassive]. Bridging this divide requires certifying active closed-loop balance stabilization as a safety-rated critical function. Demonstrating meaningful progress requires designing certifiable dynamic reaction chains—analogous to automotive emergency braking profiles—that reliably steer the robot from any arbitrary gait phase into a stable, supported configuration within bounded peak power and kinetic energy budgets. Ironically, the most capable learned machines are precisely those for which defining a safe 'stop' is most difficult.

[^fn-fail-passive-operational]: **Fail-Passive and Fail-Operational**\index{Fail-operational!balancing machine}: Avionics separates a fail-passive function, whose failure causes no significant deviation of path or attitude and hands the task back to the crew, from a fail-operational one, which keeps performing through a failure. Removing torque from a wheeled base is fail-passive in this sense, because nothing moves once the base is at rest. A balancing biped has no such state, so its posture control must remain operational until the machine reaches a supported rest, and the certifiable reaction must be a controlled one.

Contact-rich, dexterous manipulation centers on physical AI's canonical unobserved state: high-frequency contact interaction. Determining whether a snap-fit latch yields, a packaging tab seats, or a fragile container begins to crush cannot be reliably deduced from joint motor currents or external RGB-D cameras alone. High-resolution tactile sensing represents the primary modality capable of observing these hidden dynamics. Modern vision-based elastomeric tactile sensors directly capture surface deformation fields, contact geometry, and distributed shear stresses at the end-effector [@yuan2017gelsight].
However, closing the loop on contact challenges our third law (proposal is not permission). Contact forces escalate within milliseconds of initial impact (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact), far outstripping the round-trip latency of high-level neural planners and placing strict burdens on low-level passive or series elastic compliance (@sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment). The open engineering challenge is integrating tactile feedback into the formal permission path. Concrete progress requires qualifying tactile perception channels with rigorous statistical miss rates for incipient slip and shear yield, coupled with low-latency impedance controllers whose force limits can be deterministically verified and bounded by safety hardware [@tedrake2023manipulation].

Certifying learned models that directly implement safety functions constitutes the central challenge of our fourth law (evidence bounds authority). While the European Union Machinery Regulation mandates third-party notified body assessments for machine learning models executing safety-critical tasks (@sec-frontier-thesis-in-law), the robotics industry lacks standardized methodologies to certify deep neural networks at automotive or industrial safety integrity levels (SIL / PL).
Current verification techniques face stark limitations. Exact SMT-based and mixed-integer linear programming verification tools can establish formal input-output properties over declared neural network weights [@katz2017reluplex], yet these proofs remain vulnerable to the open-world modeling gaps analyzed in @sec-verification-formal-limits. Purely statistical validation collides with the exposure wall, requiring billions of physical test cycles to establish low target failure probabilities. Runtime safety filters and shield wrappers simply transfer the verification burden onto the shield's own coverage and latency envelope [@hsu2024safetyfilter]. The unresolved systems challenge is constructing hybrid safety arguments: composing analytical proofs where deterministic physics models are tractable with statistical bounds where perceptual models operate, and allocating risk budgets across both tiers. Until such composite certification arguments mature, isolating learned models outside the safety-critical permission path remains the only defensible systems posture. Verifiable progress requires publishing complete, audited conformity dossiers for learned safety components alongside their formal assurance cases.

\Needspace{24\baselineskip}

| Open problem                              | Law stressed               | Gap class             | Progress would be                                                                      | State of practice, as of 2026                                                                                                                                                                        |

| **Generalist, cross-embodiment policies** | Evidence bounds authority  | Evaluation deficit    | Evidence that transfers across bodies and updates under a stated equivalence condition | One policy across several robot types [@black2024pi0]; learning from deployment with corrections [@physicalintelligence2025recap]; motion transfer between embodiments [@geminirobotics2025gemini15] |
