The last column dates the state of practice and should be refreshed in later editions; the durable content is in the first four columns. {#tbl-17-frontier-agenda tbl-colwidths="[18,15,14,25,28]"}

Two foundational systems challenges cut across all six frontier problems:
First, continual online adaptation turns the model into a moving target. Whether a proposer retrains asynchronously on aggregated fleet telemetry or adapts its latent state online to accommodate component wear and shifting terrain [@kumar2021rma], background model updates must never starve the permission pipeline of compute or bus bandwidth.
Second, multi-robot fleet coordination tightly couples otherwise independent permission boundaries. Transmitting shared task intents across lossy wireless links cannot substitute for the local, hard-real-time sensor streams required by an individual robot's admission gate, while physically cooperative manipulation of a shared payload directly couples actuator contact dynamics across platforms.
Advancing physical AI does not require abandoning established systems rigor; it requires extending it. Unlocking the next capability begins by isolating a concrete physical task that the current system cannot safely execute, identifying the missing empirical premise or unmeasured observable, and engineering the precise evidential argument required to justify expanding the machine's operational envelope.
## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-frontier-fallacies-pitfalls}

When engineers transition physical AI systems—such as autonomous mobile manipulators in warehouses or high-speed packaging arms—from isolated algorithmic benchmarks to production floors, subtle conceptual traps frequently emerge. Even when every local calculation or trajectory optimization succeeds numerically, system-level reasoning fails if teams misunderstand the relationship between physical dynamics, learned proposers, and runtime safety enforcement. Three common fallacies and pitfalls routinely undermine embodied machine learning architectures.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A protective intervention means the whole machine failed its task.*

When a runtime safety governor or control barrier filter modifies an actuator command, engineers often mistakenly log the episode as a system-level failure. In practice, a least-change speed correction or torque clamp often allows an autonomous mobile robot or packaging arm to complete its physical mission smoothly within safe boundaries. If a warehouse robot approaches a blind turn and the protective governor trims its forward velocity from 2.0 m/s to 1.4 m/s to maintain braking margins, the delivery proceeds to completion without incident.

Treating every safety intervention as a mission failure corrupts operational telemetry. Conflating proposer interventions with unrecoverable task aborts conceals where engineering effort should be directed. Development teams must track three metrics independently: raw proposer autonomy (the fraction of time the learned model operates without override), whole-machine task success (whether the physical objective was achieved within operational deadlines), and protective intervention frequency. Decoupling these signals reveals whether system bottlenecks stem from policy distribution shift, sensor latency in the perception pipeline, or overly conservative governor tuning.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating a restriction as evidence that its physical premise holds.*

Deriving a tighter operational limit does not guarantee that the physical environment satisfies the assumptions behind that limit. For example, if an autonomous mobile robot encounters a warehouse floor contaminated by an oil film, reducing its software speed ceiling from 2.5 m/s to 1.0 m/s provides a valid stopping margin only if the tires can still achieve a minimum friction coefficient. If slick oil drops the friction coefficient toward zero, the vehicle will slide regardless of the reduced speed setpoint.

Digital artifacts cannot substitute for physical friction. Neither a signed configuration parameter in software, nor a clear path reported by an RGB camera, proves that the ground provides adequate traction. Vision pipelines readily mistake transparent oil or thin ice for dry concrete. When engineers rely on a restricted operating envelope to certify deployment safety, they must validate the physical premise through qualified measurement and environmental maintenance. This requires direct physical sensing—such as monitoring drive-wheel slip ratios and inertial deceleration—alongside site operational controls that regularly inspect and clean floor surfaces. A safety envelope is only as credible as the physical dynamics supporting it.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *More model capacity or simulated exposure settles every residual claim.*

Scaling up neural network parameter counts or running billions of simulated training steps improves policy interpolation across modeled conditions, but neither technique can overcome an unmodeled physical reality. A deep learning policy cannot infer an unobserved physical state—such as internal material stress, micro-slip at a fingertip, or variable ground compliance—if the sensor suite lacks the transducers to measure it. Similarly, physics simulators rely on simplified approximations of rigid-body contact, Coulomb friction, and non-deformable geometry. Generating massive synthetic datasets within a simulator that omits real contact mechanics merely produces policies optimized for fictitious physical dynamics.

When an embodied system displays persistent edge-case failures, the solution rarely lies in adding more transformer layers or randomizing synthetic textures. Engineers must diagnose the specific physical claim that lacks empirical grounding. Resolving the defect requires choosing the appropriate engineering intervention: integrating a dedicated physical sensor to observe the missing state, introducing passive mechanical compliance to absorb unmodeled impact energy, constraining the operational design domain, or calibrating friction models against instrumented hardware trials.
:::
## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-frontier-history}

The architectural boundaries developed throughout this chapter emerged historically from hard limits of evidence, verification, and observability. Physical systems must operate in unconstrained environments where empirical testing alone cannot provide safety guarantees. Popper established the epistemological foundation of this constraint by demonstrating that no finite sequence of observations can verify a universal hypothesis, whereas a single counterexample refutes it [@popper1959logic]. In safety-critical software engineering, Butler and Finelli formalized this evidentiary barrier as the exposure wall [@butler1993infeasibility]. They proved mathematically that certifying catastrophic failure rates on the order of $10^{-9}$ failures per operational hour requires billions of operating hours without failure—a testing volume that is physically and economically impossible for embodied systems. Decades earlier, civil aviation confronted this statistical impasse by establishing argued safety cases rather than relying solely on raw empirical testing. FAA Advisory Circular AC 25.1309 required airframers to allocate safety targets across subsystems, defining catastrophic failures as "extremely improbable" events backed by qualitative failure modes analysis and quantitative reliability budgets [@faa1988ac251309]. Modern autonomous vehicle and robotics standards build directly on this methodology: UL 4600 mandates explicit, structured safety cases connecting claims, arguments, and evidence [@ul4600], providing the disciplined engineering framework that Koopman formalizes to evaluate when an autonomous system is safe enough for public deployment [@koopman2022how].

The architectural separation between an unverified, high-capacity proposer and a deterministic permission path predates modern machine learning. In real-time fault-tolerant control, the Simplex architecture introduced by @seto1998simplex paired an unverified high-performance controller with a formally verified baseline safety controller. Simplex monitored invariant state boundaries, instantly preempting the primary controller and transferring actuation authority to the baseline fallback before the system drifted beyond its recoverable set. Sha generalized this mechanism into a fundamental principle of runtime assurance: verifiable safety requires architectural simplicity, isolating complex optimization policies from the verifiable deterministic envelopes that enforce physical invariants [@sha2001using]. Modern control theory evolved this discrete switching paradigm into continuous, minimally invasive interventions. Control barrier functions define forward-invariant safe sets, computing least-effort corrections via real-time quadratic programming to enforce state constraints while preserving policy performance [@ames2019control]. @hsu2024safetyfilter synthesize switching, reachability, and barrier mechanisms into a unified theory of safety filters. However, systems engineers must not mistake software diversity for statistical independence. Knight and Leveson demonstrated experimentally that multi-version software channels, developed independently against identical specifications, frequently exhibit correlated failures when exposed to unanticipated corner cases [@knight1986experimental]. This architectural split has since entered statutory law: the European Union's 2023 Machinery Regulation explicitly regulates safety components governed by machine learning, mandating verifiable isolation between learned optimization and deterministic protection [@eu2023machinery].

The final intellectual lineage concerns the limits of passive observation. In nonlinear dynamical systems, state distinguishability is fundamentally active rather than passive. Hermann and Krener proved that distinguishing between two candidate internal states depends strictly on the control inputs applied to the system [@hermann1977nonlinear]. Campbell and Nikoukhah operationalized this mathematical insight into active auxiliary signal design, synthesizing targeted perturbation inputs that force distinct dynamical responses between nominal and degraded operational modes within a bounded time horizon [@campbell2004auxiliary]. This chapter grounds each of these lineages directly in physical hardware execution. Abstract evidence limits become concrete risk registers backed by operational design domains and closure tests. Runtime permission logic is charged directly against physical actuation latencies, sensor staleness, and worst-case stopping distances. Finally, epistemic observation horizons translate into spatial deadlines, requiring an embodied agent to actively probe ambiguous environmental premises before physical momentum carries it past its point of safe recovery.

For further reading, six works trace the core concepts joined in this chapter:

- @butler1993infeasibility demonstrates in a few concise pages why neither black-box testing nor software reliability growth models can validate ultra-high reliability, establishing the exposure wall that bounds every statistical safety claim in physical systems.
- @leveson2011engineering formulates system safety as a dynamic control problem governing the entire sociotechnical lifecycle, providing the theoretical basis for assigning accountable owners and verifiable operational restrictions to residual hazard claims.
- @sha2001using articulates the core runtime-assurance argument that separates high-performance proposal from deterministic permission, an architectural pattern that this book develops as the foundation of safe physical AI.
- @hsu2024safetyfilter surveys modern safety filter formulations across control barrier functions, Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, and Simplex-style switching, making explicit the coverage assumptions and model fidelity priced by the shield-dilution calculations in @sec-frontier-shield-dilution.
- @campbell2004auxiliary establishes the methodology of active fault detection through designed test inputs, providing the mathematical machinery needed to probe latent environmental hypotheses before actuation deadlines expire.
- @koopman2022how presents a rigorous, practitioner-oriented framework for setting, arguing, and validating autonomous system safety goals, detailing how open risk registers and explicit safety cases replace ungrounded empirical mileage claims.
## Problems {#sec-frontier-problems}

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-problems
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GIVENS FOR THE END-OF-CHAPTER PROBLEMS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-frontier-problems.
# │ Goal:    Hold the givens the problems add to the chapter's cells: a
# │          certified gate-sensor response and a trial carriage speed, a shift
# │          log, a film arrival rate and hazard allocation, a common-cause
# │          term, traffic and trial costs on the restricted routes, a dosing
# │          valve (the process-system transfer machine), and a retraining set.
# │          Answers are not printed; the private solution script computes them.
# │ Show:    8 ms, 1.0 m/s; 1,000 / 880 / 874 / 95 / 93 / 25 / 12 / 8 moves;
# │          2e-3 and 1e-6 per hour, 1 percent; 2e-10 per hour; 40 legs/h,
# │          16 h/day, 10 min/trial; 2 L/s, 150 ms, 400 ms, 0.5 L; 10,000 images.
# │ How:     Every value is illustrative or chosen and is labeled so in the
# │          problem text; guards pin the relations the problems rely on.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import liter, minute

class FrontierProblems:
    """Givens that the chapter's problems add beyond the worked examples."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_sensor = 8 * ureg.ms  # category: illustrative (certified gate-sensor response time)
    v_trial = 1.0 * ureg.meter / ureg.second  # category: illustrative (trial carriage speed)
    n_moves = 1000  # category: illustrative (tote moves in one shift)
    n_clean = 880  # category: illustrative (every proposal admitted unchanged)
    n_clean_done = 874  # category: illustrative
    n_corrected = 95  # category: illustrative (least-change correction, no stop)
    n_corrected_done = 93  # category: illustrative
    n_stopped = 25  # category: illustrative (protective stop)
    n_stopped_resumed = 12  # category: illustrative (resumed and delivered)
    n_stopped_takeover = 8  # category: illustrative (delivered after human takeover)
    lam_film = 2e-3  # per operating hour; category: illustrative (films reaching the path)
    lam_alloc = 1e-6  # per hour; category: illustrative (hazard budget allocated to the entry)
    p_miss_relaxed = 0.01  # category: chosen (tenfold relaxation of the 0.1 percent bound)
    lam_other = 2e-10  # per hour; category: illustrative (hardware and common-cause term)
    legs_per_hour = 40  # category: illustrative (restricted-route traffic)
    hours_per_day = 16  # category: illustrative (operating hours)
    trial_time = 10 * minute  # category: illustrative (machine time per seeded-film trial)
    q_valve = 2.0  # liters per second; category: illustrative (dosing flow)
    t_valve_delay = 150 * ureg.ms  # category: illustrative (detection to close command)
    t_valve_close = 400 * ureg.ms  # category: illustrative (linear full closing time)
    v_headroom = 0.5 * liter  # category: illustrative (tank headroom above high level)
    n_images = 10_000  # category: illustrative (proposed wet-floor retraining set)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    _P = PackagingCell
    brake_chain = (_P.bus + _P.onset).to(ureg.ms)
    tau_sensor = (t_sensor + brake_chain).to(ureg.ms)
    v_sensor_ceiling = calc_max_permitted_velocity(_P.clearance, tau_sensor, _P.deceleration, physical_margin=_P.reserve).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second)
    tau_trial_max = ((_P.stop_budget - v_trial**2 / (2 * _P.deceleration)) / v_trial).to(ureg.ms)
    v_delivered = q_valve * (t_valve_delay + t_valve_close / 2).to(ureg.second).magnitude  # liters

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_clean + n_corrected + n_stopped == n_moves, "Problem 3: the shift log must account for every move.")
    check(n_stopped_resumed + n_stopped_takeover < n_stopped, "Problem 3: some stopped moves must be abandoned.")
    check(v_sensor_ceiling < v_trial < _P.v_nom, "Problem 1: the sensor ceiling must fall below the trial speed.")
    check(tau_trial_max < brake_chain, "Problem 1: the trial speed must be infeasible with the brake chain unchanged.")
    check(lam_alloc / lam_film < OilFilm.p_miss_target, "Problem 4: the derived bound must be stricter than the chosen one.")
    check(lam_other < p_target, "Problem 5: the common-cause term must leave room under the target.")
    check(v_delivered > v_headroom.to(liter).magnitude, "Problem 7: nominal flow must overfill the headroom.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_sensor_str = fmt_latency(t_sensor, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    v_trial_str = fmt_velocity(v_trial, precision=0)
    n_moves_str = fmt_int(n_moves, commas=True)
    n_clean_str = fmt_int(n_clean)
    n_clean_done_str = fmt_int(n_clean_done)
    n_corrected_str = fmt_int(n_corrected)
    n_corrected_done_str = fmt_int(n_corrected_done)
    n_stopped_str = fmt_int(n_stopped)
    n_stopped_resumed_str = fmt_int(n_stopped_resumed)
    n_stopped_takeover_str = fmt_int(n_stopped_takeover)
    lam_film_sci_str = fmt_sci(lam_film, precision=0)
    lam_alloc_sci_str = fmt_sci(lam_alloc, precision=0)
    p_miss_relaxed_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_miss_relaxed, precision=0, style="prose")
    lam_other_sci_str = fmt_sci(lam_other, precision=0)
    legs_per_hour_str = fmt_int(legs_per_hour)
    hours_per_day_str = fmt_int(hours_per_day)
    trial_time_str = fmt_latency(trial_time, unit=minute, precision=0)
    q_valve_str = fmt(q_valve, precision=0)
    t_valve_delay_str = fmt_latency(t_valve_delay, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    t_valve_close_str = fmt_latency(t_valve_close, unit=ureg.ms, precision=0)
    v_headroom_str = fmt_water(v_headroom, unit=liter, precision=1)
    n_images_str = fmt_int(n_images, commas=True)
```

The following problems apply the chapter's physical AI principles to concrete engineering decisions. They extend the warehouse transport machine and the high-speed packaging cell, using illustrative parameters that stand in for physical plant measurements. Each exercise identifies the specific architectural or operational decision required. The bracketed tags designate the mode of analysis—computation, design, or critique—along with the corresponding learning objectives assessed. @Tbl-17-key-equations summarizes the primary governing equations, their operational significance, and where this book derives them.

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}

| Equation                                                                                                                                | What it bounds or decides                                                         | Where derived                                                      |
|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| $d_{\text{stop}} = v\tau_{\text{delay}} + v^2/2a_{\text{brake}}$                                                                        | Whether a mode's stop fits its clearance, and whether delay or braking dominates  | @eq-body-stopping-distance                                         |
| $v_{\max} = -a_{\text{brake}}\tau_{\text{delay}} + \sqrt{(a_{\text{brake}}\tau_{\text{delay}})^2 + 2a_{\text{brake}}d_{\text{budget}}}$ | The speed ceiling a stopping budget admits                                        | @eq-body-velocity-ceiling; jerk ramps in @eq-enforce-speed-ceiling |
| $a = \min(a_{\text{brake}}, \mu g)$                                                                                                     | Whether the brake or the floor binds, and the friction floor $a_{\text{brake}}/g$ | @eq-frontier-credible-deceleration                                 |
| $\lambda_{\text{system},h} \le \lambda_{\text{proposal},h}(1-c_h) + \lambda_{\text{other}}$                                             | What a shield adds to a hazard-rate claim, and the coverage the claim needs       | @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard                                       |
| $n = \lceil \ln\alpha / \ln(1-p) \rceil$                                                                                                | Failure-free trials that bound a miss or false-accept probability $p$             | @eq-eval-zero-failure-sample-size                                  |
| $d_{\text{detect}} \ge v\,t_{\text{detect}} + d_{\text{budget}}(v)$                                                                     | The range at which a detector must report a hazard ahead of the machine           | @eq-frontier-film-detection-range                                  |
| $d_{\text{rem}} \ge v\,(t_{\text{enforce}} + t_{\text{actuation}}) + d_{\text{brake}}(v)$                                               | The latest point at which a distinguishing observation can still help             | @eq-frontier-action-deadline                                       |
| $F_{\text{trip}} + k_{\text{eq}}\,\Delta x_{\text{driven}} \le F_{\text{floor}}$                                                        | The stiffness of a passive element that bounds contact force                      | @eq-frontier-passive-compliance                                    |

: **Key equations of the chapter**: Each equation the chapter applies to the warehouse machine or the packaging cell, what it bounds or decides, and where the book derives it. The first two and the zero-failure count are derived in earlier chapters and reused here; the others are stated in this chapter. {#tbl-17-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[42,36,22]"}

1. **[Compute, LO3] A certified gate sensor.** On a production packaging cell, a safety-rated gate interlock sensor triggering Safe Stop 1 (SS1) replaces the camera-triggered stop (@sec-frontier-packaging-cell-study). Suppose its illustrative certified response time of `{python} FrontierProblems.t_sensor_str` replaces the image acquisition and processing allocations, while the `{python} PackagingCell.bus_str` command delivery delay, `{python} PackagingCell.onset_str` brake torque buildup, `{python} PackagingCell.deceleration_str` braking bound, and `{python} PackagingCell.stop_budget_str` stopping budget remain unchanged. Compute the new carriage velocity ceiling. Determine whether any gate sensor could admit an illustrative trial speed of `{python} FrontierProblems.v_trial_str` with the mechanical brake chain unchanged, and calculate the braking bound required to admit the `{python} PackagingCell.v_nom_str` nominal speed even under zero sensor delay. Finally, name the physical subsystem investment that the packaging cell's throughput goal demands.
2. **[Compute, LO3, LO5] How far the inspected floor may fall.** The claims register entry for surface oil films admits a restricted speed of `{python} OilFilm.v_restricted_str` on warehouse floors inspected to maintain a surface friction coefficient of $\mu \ge$ `{python} OilFilm.mu_insp_str`. Using the complete stopping budget from \ref{nbk-frontier-friction-floor} along with its established sensing delay, jerk bound, and overheads, find the friction coefficient below which this restricted mode exceeds the `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance. State the safety margin that the routine inspection regime preserves below `{python} OilFilm.mu_insp_str`. Finally, write the formal pass/fail acceptance criterion that an automated friction survey along a served route must satisfy for the register entry to continue admitting this restricted mode.
3. **[Compute, LO4] Three outcomes from one shift.** An illustrative shift log for the autonomous warehouse machine records `{python} FrontierProblems.n_moves_str` tote transport dispatches. In `{python} FrontierProblems.n_clean_str` of these moves, the safety shield admitted every proposal unchanged, and `{python} FrontierProblems.n_clean_done_str` were delivered successfully. In `{python} FrontierProblems.n_corrected_str` moves, the permission path applied a least-change speed clamp without stopping the vehicle, and `{python} FrontierProblems.n_corrected_done_str` completed delivery. In `{python} FrontierProblems.n_stopped_str` moves, the system triggered a protective stop: `{python} FrontierProblems.n_stopped_resumed_str` resumed autonomously and were delivered, `{python} FrontierProblems.n_stopped_takeover_str` were delivered only after manual operator intervention, and the remainder were abandoned. Compute the raw proposer autonomy rate, whole-machine task success both with and without takeover-assisted deliveries, and the protective-response rate. Compare these metrics against a blunt single count that classifies every intervention as a failure. Finally, decide whether the next engineering improvement belongs in proposer policy learning, system integration, or the protective-stop recovery workflow.
4. **[Compute, LO5, LO6] Deriving the miss bound.** Rather than adopting the claims register's preselected miss bound of `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_pct_str` for the floor-film detector, derive a target from operational hazard allocations. Suppose site spill records indicate that lubricant films enter the vehicle's path at an illustrative rate of `{python} FrontierProblems.lam_film_sci_str` per operating hour across served routes, and the facility safety case allocates this specific hazard entry an illustrative budget of `{python} FrontierProblems.lam_alloc_sci_str` per hour. Find the maximum permissible miss probability that the detector must meet, along with the number of consecutive failure-free physical trials needed to bound it at `{python} OilFilm.confidence_pct_str` statistical confidence. Compare your result with the preselected bound and with a relaxed bound of `{python} FrontierProblems.p_miss_relaxed_pct_str`, calculating the residual film-hazard rate each alternative leaves against the allocated budget.
5. **[Compute, LO6] Coverage with a common-cause term.** Revisit the residual hazard calculation in \ref{nbk-frontier-fleet-exposure-and-shielded-decomposition}, this time including an illustrative hardware and common-cause failure rate of $\lambda_{\text{other}} =$ `{python} FrontierProblems.lam_other_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$ rather than assuming an idealized zero. Determine the shield coverage $c$ that the system hazard target demands given the `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.confidence_pct_str` proposal bound, and find the sample size of the seeded-trial campaign needed to certify that coverage. Recompute both values under a conservative Bonferroni confidence split. Finally, calculate the critical threshold for $\lambda_{\text{other}}$ above which no degree of shield coverage can satisfy the target, and explain what form of engineering evidence must change when this hardware floor binds.
6. **[Compute, LO6] When to buy the closure test.** In @sec-frontier-deployment-economics, the operational cost of the oil-film operating restriction was priced per `{python} RestrictionCost.leg_str` aisle leg. Suppose that across restricted routes, the vehicle completes an illustrative `{python} FrontierProblems.legs_per_hour_str` legs per operating hour over `{python} FrontierProblems.hours_per_day_str` operating hours each day. Concurrently, executing each seeded-film test run in the `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str`-trial empirical closure campaign consumes an illustrative `{python} FrontierProblems.trial_time_str` of dedicated machine time. Express both the daily penalty of the operating restriction and the total expenditure of the validation campaign in machine-hours. Compute the operational break-even period for the validation campaign, and recompute this payoff horizon assuming route traffic falls by half. Finally, identify what operational data the facility team must verify before authorizing the capital expenditure for the closure campaign.
7. **[Compute, LO3] Transfer to a dosing valve.** The process-system case study in @sec-frontier-packaging-cell-study features a learned neural network proposer setting the opening of an industrial dosing valve feeding a tank. The illustrative fluid flow rate is `{python} FrontierProblems.q_valve_str` liters per second, the sensing and processing delay from a tank high-level trip to the valve closure command is `{python} FrontierProblems.t_valve_delay_str`, and the valve closes linearly over `{python} FrontierProblems.t_valve_close_str` (passing an average of half its full flow during actuation). The receiving vessel provides `{python} FrontierProblems.v_headroom_str` of volumetric headroom above the high-level trip threshold. Compute the total liquid volume delivered into the tank after a high-level event occurs. Determine the highest flow rate whose overrun volume fits within the available headroom, and recompute this flow ceiling assuming either the mechanical closing time or the control delay is halved. Finally, decide the fail-safe state that the valve actuator must assume upon total loss of electrical power, and state what mechanical relief mechanism the qualified fallback must specify if the upstream feed line remains pressurized.
8. **[Design, LO3, LO5] A humanoid at a tote wall.** A bipedal humanoid robot extracts totes from a high shelving wall and carries them across a facility floor shared with human pedestrians to reach a staging cart. Apply the causal boundary scope test from @sec-boundary and the four-law audit protocol from @sec-frontier-four-law-audit-protocol to this operation. Deliver a structured audit table with columns for Claim, Premise, Status (using one of the five classifications defined in the Reader's Guide), and Verdict, providing explicit evaluation rows for walking transport, shelf tote picking, and the protective response upon loss of execution permission. In addition, draft at least two formal residual-claims register entries. Because numerical plant parameters are not specified, explicitly label every assumed input as either chosen or illustrative. Finally, explain why the wheeled vehicle's zero-velocity stop-and-hold fallback fails to provide a viable safe state for an unconstrained bipedal gait (@sec-frontier-four-open-challenges), and identify which specific safety claims your audit table must therefore reject.
9. **[Design, LO5, LO6] Register entries for the packaging cell.** Draft formal residual-claims register entries for two packaging cell failure modes: carton tab engagement under severe optical glare, and motor winding thermal duty during continuous high-cadence cycling. For each entry, specify the unobserved physical state, the mandatory operating restriction, the accountable engineering owner, and a predeclared closure test, categorizing each by its epistemic gap class (@sec-frontier-four-gap-classes). For the thermal duty entry, identify the key physical wear mechanisms that the hardware's `{python} PackagingCell.temperature_trip_str` temperature trip and `{python} PackagingCell.stall_timeout_str` stall timeout fail to observe directly. Finally, state what an empirical closure test must demonstrate regarding cumulative winding insulation degradation and dielectric breakdown rather than instantaneous operating temperature.
10. **[Critique, LO1] Retraining on wet floors.** An engineering team proposes closing the oil-film claims register entry by retraining the vision navigation network on `{python} FrontierProblems.n_images_str` labeled images of wet and specular warehouse floors. Critique this proposal using the friction dynamics from \ref{nbk-frontier-friction-floor} and the third fallacy analyzed in @sec-frontier-fallacies-pitfalls. Clearly distinguish between the epistemic claim that image dataset retraining can legitimately substantiate and the physical dynamics claim that it cannot. Finally, identify what empirical evidence the formal closure test in @tbl-17-claims-register still requires regarding real-world braking force and stopping distances before the operational restriction can be lifted.
11. **[Critique, LO2] Capable enough to drive the actuators.** A robotics vendor claims that its next cross-embodiment foundation policy halves the rate of hazardous trajectory proposals, arguing that this reliability gain justifies eliminating the independent permission path and routing neural network action commands directly to actuator motor drives. Critique this architectural change using the shielded hazard formulation from @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard and the legal accountability thesis from @sec-frontier-thesis-in-law. Determine the residual hazard rate that results when the architectural shield is removed ($c_h = 0$). Evaluate the empirical sample size needed to statistically certify this halving against the fleet exposure wall, and identify which specific conformity assessment route the unshielded machine architecture must pursue under the European Union Machinery Regulation.
12. **[Critique, LO5] Ranking operators by takeovers.** A facility operations manager proposes ranking floor supervisors by their recorded manual takeover counts in the machine's authority log, tying annual performance bonuses to low takeover frequencies. Critique this proposal using the workforce accountability principles of @sec-frontier-workforce-accountability. Detail what confounding physical and system variables a takeover count reflects beyond the operator's vigilance, such as localized traction loss, transient sensor occlusions, or overly conservative shield margins. Outline the regulatory obligations and compliance burdens that the European Union AI Act imposes on automated systems deployed for worker evaluation and monitoring. Finally, explain how establishing a declared purpose, designated engineering owner, and restricted readership for the authority log protects the integrity of safety reporting and prevents dangerous gaming of the control handoff.
## Summary {#sec-frontier-summary}

The warehouse mobile manipulator now possesses a complete, connected design argument, and the high-speed packaging cell demonstrates how to transfer that argument to an unfamiliar machine. Across seventeen chapters, this book has traced the systems discipline demanded when machine learning moves from disembodied computation to physical agency. The journey began at the causal boundary, stepping past the digital glass of advisory inference and virtual software sandboxes into a physical world governed by continuous dynamics, thermodynamics, and the irreversible flow of time. Where digital systems could rely on transactional rollback, unconstrained test-time deliberation, and batch processing, embodied machines must govern single-batch execution ($B=1$) under hard real-time deadlines where every millisecond of computational delay translates irrevocably into physical distance traveled.

The book opened by asking why a better prediction can still produce a worse physical action. This chapter's synthesis provides the definitive answer. A neural network optimizes expected statistical loss over its training distribution, but the physical plant operates under continuous Newtonian mechanics, electromagnetism, and thermodynamics. A better proposer cannot supply the friction premise that an unobserved oil film removes, because no input it receives measures the tire-ground contact interface. It cannot make a derated operating mode evaluated, because the operational restriction that shortens the stop also displaces the proposer into physical configurations its training and evaluation never sampled. It cannot close a detectorless claim such as the glare-hidden packaging tab, because the physical sensor required to resolve that state does not exist on the machine. Nor can a faster forward pass recover the stopping distance already consumed while the vehicle cruised under unguided momentum ($d = v \tau_{\text{delay}}$). In each case, the physical outcome is judged by dynamics, timing, and environmental evidence that the learned prediction does not contain.

For this reason, the learned model must be engineered as an unprivileged component of a machine rather than as the machine itself. The rest of the machine supplies what the statistical model lacks, one law at a time:

- Under the first law (*irreversibility*), the Body establishes immutable kinetic, actuator, and thermal budgets that bound what any proposal may request.
- Under the second law (*endogenous data*), the closed loop recognizes that actions dictate subsequent observations, requiring that policy competence be evaluated on the empirical state distribution induced by physical execution and that only qualified new experience can expand the operational design domain.
- Under the third law (*proposal is not permission*), the proposal boundary separates the speculative Brain from an independent, deterministic Nervous System that polices the causal boundary, enforcing forward-invariant safety envelopes and maintaining an assured fallback on isolated real-time silicon.
- Under the fourth law (*evidence bounds authority*), operational governance ensures that authority never exceeds accumulated empirical evidence, codifying unobserved physical states, mandatory operational restrictions, accountable engineering owners, and predeclared closure tests in a formal residual-claims register.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Engineering a machine that senses and acts"}

* **Useful service joins the four laws:** Body limits, learned competence, independent permission, and maintained evidence must support the same task; a better prediction strengthens only one link of that argument.
* **Competence can grow:** New qualified experience, retraining, and regression evaluation can extend what the next candidate can justify.
* **Admission can preserve success:** A minimally corrected proposal can complete useful work; proposer autonomy, task success, and protection require separate measures.
* **Restrictions need evidence:** A lower speed still needs traction, clearance, and a feasible response. A stipulated supported branch teaches the release decision without turning illustrative records into measurements.
* **Residual limits select the next experiment:** Missing observations, evaluation support, proof premises, and task scope call for different engineering responses.
:::

A physical AI engineer can carry an intended task through this entire chain. The engineer derives an action envelope from the body and its environment, develops a learned proposer from traceable data, and evaluates that proposer in the closed loop it will inhabit. The engineer then integrates sensing, state, intent, and planning with an independent permission path, measures its timing and fallback behavior, and tests the complete machine under declared operating conditions. The release decision joins useful capability to the evidence that supports it. When evidence is missing, the engineer can identify whether the next step is a physical measurement, a learning experiment, an architectural change, or a narrower operational domain. @Sec-boundary promised the ability to design, teach, integrate, evaluate, and maintain such a machine within justified operating limits, and to name, when the evidence is incomplete, what would support the next capability. That ability to build, verify, and justify a machine that senses and acts is the enduring discipline this book develops.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From physical AI to the systems discipline"}
The next unfamiliar machine will bring a different body, task, and environment. Its engineering begins by tracing how observations become proposals and how admitted commands become force, motion, and heat. The methods developed here provide a way to teach useful behavior, integrate it with timely physical control, and determine which operating claims the resulting evidence supports. This work is dedicated to the students, researchers, and systems engineers who take up the challenge of giving machines safe and capable hands in an open physical world.
:::
